item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library with a formation manager that supplies individual target locations from a common pattern and anchor.
item0.explanation: Formation keeps member-to-slot assignments and delegates their updates to a strategy. In updateSlots it obtains each pattern-relative target, rotates it by the anchor’s orientation, adds the anchor translation with any drift correction, and writes the result to the member’s target location. An optional motion moderator can update the anchor. Members must still move towards those targets in other game code; publishing slots alone does not enforce speed or collision constraints.

intuition.text: The harbour launcher can predict where a shot lands without firing it. Treat its signed miss as feedback: a short prediction and a long prediction surround a useful angle, and each new prediction narrows that choice. The important result is an angle with a measured small miss, rather than an attractive-looking arc.
intuition.situation: A training launcher must hit a stationary drum while its game’s drag rule changes the flight. Reusing that flight rule inside the aiming search keeps the prediction consistent with the toy physics.

example.name: The harbour launcher finding the drum
example.description: The drum is {targetX} m along level ground. Every candidate leaves the harbour launcher at {launchSpeed} m/s; only its angle changes between {lowerAngle}° and {upperAngle}°. The local simulator uses downward gravity {gravity} m/s², linear drag coefficient {drag} per second and velocity-before-position steps of {timeStep} s. Two endpoint probes precede at most {maxIterations} midpoint guesses. A completed impact within {tolerance} m is accepted; {flightSteps} physics steps bound each prediction. The drawing currently shows angle {angle}°, signed miss {error} m and search status {status}.

step0.title: Require a useful angle bracket
step0.text: Predict the endpoint shots first. Both must reach the ground. Accept an endpoint already within tolerance; otherwise their signed range errors must surround zero. A same-side pair rejects this bracket, rather than declaring the drum unreachable at every possible angle. Endpoint probes are separate from the midpoint-guess budget.

step1.title: Predict the midpoint shot
step1.text: Bisect the current angles {bracketLower}° and {bracketUpper}° to obtain {angle}°. Resolve the fixed launch speed into horizontal and vertical velocity, then repeatedly apply gravity and drag. Interpolate the first ground crossing between the surrounding samples so the miss is measured on the ground, rather than at the last airborne point.

step2.title: Measure before accepting
step2.text: Subtract the drum position from the predicted impact: {impactX} − {targetX} = {error} m. Positive means long and negative means short. Accept only when the absolute miss is at most {tolerance} m. A prediction that outlasts its physics horizon has an unknown impact, not a successful shot.

step3.title: Retain the sign change or report failure
step3.text: Compare the midpoint’s sign with the lower endpoint’s sign and discard the half without a sign change. The candidate next bracket is [{nextLower}, {nextUpper}]°. Repeat until acceptance or the budget ends. Exhausting a budget with a remaining miss reports failure even when the next guess might have succeeded.

pseudocode.ordinary:
lowFlight = simulate(lowerAngle)
highFlight = simulate(upperAngle)
if either flight has no ground impact: fail unfinished
lowError = lowFlight.range - targetX
highError = highFlight.range - targetX
if abs(lowError) <= tolerance: accept lowerAngle
if abs(highError) <= tolerance: accept upperAngle
if lowError * highError > 0: fail unbracketed

angle = (lowerAngle + upperAngle) / 2
velocity = launchSpeed * (cos(angle), sin(angle))
repeat at most flightSteps times:
  vx = vx + (-drag * vx) * dt
  vy = vy + (-gravity - drag * vy) * dt
  nextPosition = position + (vx, vy) * dt
  if nextHeight <= 0:
    fraction = height / (height - nextHeight)
    range = x + fraction * (nextX - x)
    end this prediction
  position = nextPosition

if no ground crossing: fail unfinished
error = range - targetX
if abs(error) <= tolerance: accept angle

if lowError * error > 0:
  lowerAngle = angle
  lowError = error
else:
  upperAngle = angle
repeat midpoint prediction while guesses remain
otherwise report budget exhausted

visual.textEquivalent: Search step {iteration} predicts a shot at {angle}° from the harbour launcher towards the drum at {targetX} m: impact {impactX} m after {flightTime} s of simulated flight, signed miss {error} m, current bracket [{bracketLower}, {bracketUpper}]°, next bracket [{nextLower}, {nextUpper}]°, status {status}.

item1.title: GNU Scientific Library · One Dimensional Root-Finding
item1.supports: Bisection evaluates an interval midpoint and keeps a half selected by sign; bracketing needs a zero crossing, and convergence tests and iteration limits are separate stopping conditions. This is numerical-method support, not a projectile implementation.

limits.item0: The search solves its own fixed-step flight model. A different integration order, drag law or collision rule in the game can turn a small predicted miss into a real miss; tightening the search tolerance cannot remove that modelling error.
limits.item1: Reducing the midpoint budget to {shortBudget} can stop with a measurable miss outside tolerance. The comparison holds the last result after stopping; it does not imply the solver continued working.
limits.item2: Endpoint signs establish a bracket only for a continuous range-error function. Terrain collisions, target switching or discontinuous flight rules can invalidate that assumption. Same-side endpoint errors do not prove there is no intermediate or higher-arc solution.
limits.item3: The drum stays still on level ground. Moving targets require impact-time prediction, and this local angle search does not choose between low and high arcs or check obstacles along an arc.
limits.item4: This study-local search and linear-drag simulator are absent from the public scene engine. The engine supplies only deterministic trigonometry here; no whole-scene projectile behaviour is claimed.

item0.why: Read Projectiles with drag when the main uncertainty is the force and integration model that each candidate prediction should run.

item1.why: Use The firing solution when the chosen physics admits a direct launch calculation and repeated flight guesses are unnecessary.

item2.why: Two-arc ambiguity matters when more than one launch angle can reach the drum and clearance or flight time must choose between them.

item3.why: Moving targets adds the changing destination at the predicted impact time; the stationary drum’s range error is then insufficient.

intuition.text: A take-off marker asks Finch to arrive in a particular moving state. Reaching the painted ring while standing still is no help when the canal crossing needs forward speed. The run-up prepares that speed; the marker grants the vertical jump only when position and velocity agree with its requirement.
intuition.situation: A courier follows a straight quay towards a designer-authored crossing. The marker makes the transition from ground locomotion to airborne motion inspectable and gives an explicit reason to refuse a poorly prepared jump.

example.name: Finch crossing the canal
example.description: Finch begins at {startX} m with horizontal velocity {initialVelocity} m/s and approaches the take-off ring at {markerX} m. The ring requires {requiredVelocity} m/s within {velocityTolerance} m/s and position within {positionTolerance} m. Run-up acceleration is limited to {maxAcceleration} m/s², speed to {maxSpeed} m/s and response time to {responseTime} s. An accepted launch adds vertical velocity {verticalVelocity} m/s under gravity {gravity} m/s². The equal-height receiving pad is centred at {padCentre} m, with half-width {padHalfWidth} m. The current phase is {phase}, horizontal speed {vx} m/s and height {height} m.

step0.title: Author a take-off state
step0.text: Place the ring at {markerX} m and require forward velocity {requiredVelocity} m/s. For this canal, the vertical impulse and equal platform heights imply flight duration {flightDuration} s. Place the receiving pad where that required horizontal velocity carries Finch during the flight. The marker protocol and this trajectory are study-local.

step1.title: Prepare the moving arrival
step1.text: During the straight run-up, call the scene engine’s matchVelocity with the marker’s required velocity. It requests the velocity gap divided by {responseTime} s and caps acceleration. Advance the new horizontal velocity over {timeStep} s. This is a velocity target, so the run-up keeps moving through the ring rather than slowing towards a stop.

step2.title: Check both conditions at the marker
step2.text: At the first sampled encounter with the marker window, check position error and horizontal velocity error together. Only a valid state receives the vertical launch impulse; preserve the actual horizontal velocity instead of replacing it with the requested one. A failed encounter ends this one-pass example as rejected, with no claim to simulate emergency braking.

step3.title: Follow the accepted flight
step3.text: After take-off, horizontal velocity remains constant and height follows the constant-gravity equation. Sample until the equal-height ground contact, then compare the contact position with the receiving pad. The airborne calculation uses elapsed flight time {airTime} s; the current height is {height} m and vertical velocity {vy} m/s. The study stops before landing collision response.

pseudocode.ordinary:
marker = (markerX, requiredVelocity)
flightDuration = 2 * verticalVelocity / gravity
padCentre = markerX + requiredVelocity * flightDuration
state = (startX, initialVelocity, runUp)

while x < markerX - positionTolerance and steps remain:
  acceleration = engine.matchVelocity(body, requiredVelocity, responseTime)
  velocity = clamp(velocity + acceleration * dt, -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)
  x = x + velocity * dt
if the step horizon ends before the marker: report unfinished

positionOK = abs(x - markerX) <= positionTolerance
velocityOK = abs(velocity - requiredVelocity) <= velocityTolerance
if not (positionOK and velocityOK): reject this encounter
takeoffX = x
takeoffVelocity = velocity
apply verticalVelocity as the jump impulse

for each airborne sample t through flightDuration:
  x = takeoffX + takeoffVelocity * t
  height = verticalVelocity * t - gravity * t * t / 2
  vy = verticalVelocity - gravity * t
at ground contact:
  landingError = abs(x - padCentre)
  report whether landingError <= padHalfWidth
  end before collision response

visual.textEquivalent: At {seconds} s Finch is in phase {phase}, x {x} m and height {height} m, with horizontal velocity {vx} m/s and vertical velocity {vy} m/s; the ring at {markerX} m requires {requiredVelocity} m/s, current position error is {positionError} m and velocity error {velocityError} m/s, while the planned arc ends at the receiving pad centred at {padCentre} m.

item2.title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1 · §4.3 Projectile Motion
item2.supports: Under constant downward gravity and negligible air resistance, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical position is initial vertical velocity times time minus half gravity times time squared; equal-height flight duration follows from that equation.

limits.item0: A marker does not supply the runway needed to reach its required velocity. Starting at {lateStartX} m can reach the ring with too much velocity error; the comparison rejects launch rather than silently supplying the missing horizontal speed.
limits.item1: The runway is straight and aligned with the required velocity. This one-dimensional run-up uses engine velocity matching, not a general controller that synchronises an arbitrary position and velocity in space.
limits.item2: The gate is tested at sampled positions. A coarse step can skip a narrow position window even with the correct speed; the one-pass policy then rejects the encounter. A production controller could plan an event crossing or retry, but neither occurs here.
limits.item3: An accepted state is within tolerances, rather than necessarily exact. Its actual launch position and velocity determine contact, so an especially narrow receiving pad can still be missed.
limits.item4: The flight assumes equal platform heights, constant gravity and no air resistance or mid-air control. The terminal sample ends at contact before collision response; this local marker protocol is not a scene-engine jumping feature.

item0.why: Landing pads becomes useful when the receiving region and its tolerances should determine the launch requirement, rather than merely checking this authored crossing.

item1.why: Velocity matching explains the engine acceleration that prepares the run-up; use it alone when matching motion is enough and no jump transition is needed.

item2.why: Take-off velocity matching focuses on reaching the required moving state, especially when the runway, acceleration limit or timing makes that state difficult to obtain.

item3.why: Arrive is appropriate when Finch should stop at a destination. A launch marker instead requires forward motion at the encounter.

intuition.text: The archive trolley treats its remaining journey as a fresh request at every update: cover the gap within the chosen response time. Far from the charger, that request exceeds its speed cap. Nearby, the same calculation asks for less speed. The trolley adopts the requested velocity immediately, so its slowing comes from smaller requests rather than simulated braking.
intuition.situation: A trolley in an archive animation needs to approach its charging marker smoothly, while the animation can set its velocity directly.

example.name: The archive trolley approaches its charger
example.description: The trolley starts at {start} on a straight aisle and heads for a charging marker at {target}. Its speed cap is {maxSpeed} units/s, time to target {timeToTarget} s and satisfaction radius {satisfactionRadius} units. Each update advances {timeStep} s; the run contains {steps} updates. The outer circle has the derived radius {taperDistance}, where the speed cap stops binding. This executable uses a study-local velocity rule: the public scene engine has acceleration-based Arrive, but no direct-velocity kinematic arrival helper.

step0.title: Measure the signed journey left
step0.text: Subtract the trolley position from the marker position. The sign chooses the direction of travel; the magnitude is the distance used by the stop decision. At this moment the trolley is at {position}, leaving {distance} units.

step1.title: Accept a region, keeping its error
step1.text: This model includes the boundary: distance at or below {satisfactionRadius} units accepts the current place. It assigns zero velocity and leaves the trolley there. Acceptance does not place it exactly on the marker, and it can stop immediately because the model carries no momentum.

step2.title: Turn the remaining journey into velocity
step2.text: Outside the accepted region, divide the signed offset by {timeToTarget} s and clamp the result to the speed cap. No separate slowing-radius input is needed: tapering begins at maxSpeed × timeToTarget, currently {taperDistance} units from the marker. The assigned velocity now is {velocity} units/s.

step3.title: Advance with that assigned velocity
step3.text: Multiply velocity by the update duration, then add the displacement to position. This update moves {displacement} units to {nextPosition}. Where the speed cap is inactive and the stop has not been accepted, the next signed error equals the old error multiplied by 1 − dt / timeToTarget, currently {errorFactor}.

visual.textEquivalent: The archive trolley is at {position}, {distance} units from the charging marker at {target}; it is {accepted}, assigns velocity {velocity} units/s and will move {displacement} units to {nextPosition}, with an outer taper circle of radius {taperDistance} and an inner acceptance circle of radius {satisfactionRadius}.

item0.relevance: aicore is a C++ game-AI library containing a concrete KinematicArrive implementation. Its maintainer labels the repository historical and says it has not kept pace with the third edition, so it is a readable implementation rather than a current book reference.
item0.explanation: KinematicArrive computes the target offset, clears its linear output inside a strict squared-radius test, otherwise divides the offset by timeToTarget and caps its magnitude at maxSpeed. The accompanying header describes kinematic output as a velocity reached immediately. This makes the direct velocity contract explicit; the routine itself does not advance the character position.

intuition.text: Moss, a gallery patrol robot, keeps walking while its facing drifts. Each update remembers the previous facing and adds a small signed turn. That memory gives the trail continuity: choosing an entirely new compass direction would make each update unrelated to the last.
intuition.situation: Use this when an idle character should roam without a destination and its movement system accepts velocity directly. It gives Moss motion to watch; it does not give the patrol a route or a guarantee of visiting every room.

example.name: Moss patrols an empty gallery
example.description: Moss starts at ({startX}, {startY}), facing {startHeading} radians, and immediately walks at {speed} units/s. Every {timeStep} s it draws a signed turn rate bounded by {maxRotation} radians/s. Seed {seed} makes the {duration}-second patrol replayable. The comparison raises only the turn-rate bound to {failureRotation} radians/s. The empty gallery has no walls or stopping rule.

step0.title: Read the current facing as velocity
step0.text: Convert the remembered angle with the public engine's deterministic cosine and sine, normalise the direction and multiply by {speed}. Moss uses this velocity immediately; there is no acceleration ramp. The green arrow is this update's displacement direction.

step1.title: Draw a small signed turn
step1.text: Take the difference of successive uniform draws. Small differences are more common than extreme ones; the sign chooses a turning direction. Multiplying by {maxRotation} gives a turn rate. The seeded generator is study-local because the engine's random helpers are not public exports.

step2.title: Move, then remember the new facing
step2.text: Move with the velocity calculated from the old facing, then add turnRate × {timeStep} to that facing. The amber arrow previews the next update's velocity. This direct kinematic update is study-local: the public engine's wander function is an acceleration-based behaviour with a forward circle, a different mechanism.

pseudocode.ordinary:
direction = normalize({ x: cosine(heading), y: sine(heading) })
velocity = direction * speed

[first, seed] = seededUniform(seed)
[second, seed] = seededUniform(seed)
sample = first - second
turnRate = sample * maxRotation

position = position + velocity * timeStep
heading = heading + turnRate * timeStep
remember(position, heading, seed)

visual.textEquivalent: At {seconds} s, Moss is at ({x}, {y}), facing {heading} radians and moving at {currentSpeed} units/s; the green velocity is ({velocityX}, {velocityY}), {turnDescription}, and the amber next-update direction faces {nextHeading} radians.

item0.relevance: This public C# teaching collection supplies Unity components for classic movement behaviours. Its kinematic wander component exposes speed, rotation range and separate waiting periods for turning and translation.
item0.explanation: RandomBinomial subtracts two floating-point uniform draws. Separate coroutines set rotation and translate along the object's forward vector. Rotation is assigned as an absolute Euler angle rather than accumulated, and translation is a distance per coroutine iteration without elapsed-time scaling. Those choices make its clocks and units part of its behaviour; the file is an implementation to inspect, with limits visible in its code.

intuition.text: Fern needs to look like a creature the player can influence. Keeping company, leaving room, drifting about and moving away from the player are separate requests for acceleration. Giving sheep and goats different strengths for those requests creates different responses from the same controller. The design work is deciding which requests apply, whom each creature observes and what happens when the requests conflict.
intuition.situation: Kit drives the sheep Fern and Moss and the goats Flint and Pebble east through Bracken Meadow. Each species has its own profile; adjust the player response and the goats' wander weight to see how those choices change the drive. These are chosen game personalities, not measured animal traits.

example.name: The Bracken Meadow drive
example.description: Kit follows a fixed eastward path. The creatures start still: Fern and Moss form the inner pair, Flint and Pebble the outer pair. They separate from either species but cohere and match velocity only with nearby members of their own species. Player response has scale {fleeScale}; goat wandering has weight {goatWander}, against the sheep's {sheepWander}. Both profiles call the scene engine's separation, arrive, matchVelocity, wander, flee and blend functions. Profile selection, perception, the prescribed wander-angle wobble and the simultaneous fixed-step update are study-local. Distances use arbitrary field units, time uses seconds and angles use radians; the engine's fixed flee range is {fleeRadius} units.

step0.title: Sample Kit and the creature neighbourhoods
step0.text: Kit is {playerRelation} the sheep. Fern reads {neighbours} sheep neighbours, excluding herself when averaging their positions and velocities. Same-species membership affects cohesion and alignment; separation still considers goats. Each creature reads the old frame, before anyone moves.

step1.title: Select a profile without changing the algorithm
step1.text: The sheep profile uses wander weight {sheepWander} and effective flee weight {sheepFlee}; the goat profile uses {goatWander} and {goatFlee}. Effective flee weight is the species weight times fleeScale, the input changed in the comparison. The common spacing and velocity rules keep the same implementation for both profiles.

step2.title: Build the social requests
step2.text: Engine separate uses linear falloff over close creatures. Engine arrive heads towards the same-species centre with a point target and a slowing radius, while engine matchVelocity closes the gap to the neighbours' mean velocity. Empty social neighbourhoods silence cohesion and alignment. The Social row adds these weighted requests; their individual directions and values appear in the worked step.

step3.title: Add wandering and the player response
step3.text: A deterministic sine wobble sets Fern's wander angle to {angle} radians; paired creatures use opposite signs. Engine wander selects a velocity along its projected circle and corrects towards it. Engine flee points away from Kit, fading to nothing at the fixed {fleeRadius}-unit range. Fern is {gap} units away; her weighted wander and flee requests have magnitudes {wanderMagnitude} and {fleeMagnitude} units/s².

step4.title: Resolve all requests with a weighted sum
step4.text: Engine blend multiplies the social, wander and flee outputs by their selected weights, adds them and caps the result at {maxAcceleration} units/s². Fern's result has magnitude {accelerationMagnitude} units/s². No request has automatic precedence: increasing flee strengthens a contribution but does not turn the blend into a safety constraint.

step5.title: Integrate together and measure the response
step5.text: Update each velocity over {timeStep} seconds, cap speed and move with the updated velocity, then publish the whole new frame. Kit's next position comes from the same fixed path. The chart shows signed eastward centre displacements of {sheepTravel} units for sheep and {goatTravel} for goats; these measure the profiles' effects on this drive.

pseudocode.ordinary:
old = snapshot(creatures)
seconds = step * timeStep
player = (playerStartX + playerSpeed * seconds, playerY)
for each body in old:
  neighbours = other bodies of body.species strictly within neighbourRadius
  centre, meanVelocity = means of neighbours when nonempty

  profile = sheepProfile when body.species is sheep, otherwise goatProfile
  wanderWeight = profile.wanderWeight
  fleeWeight = profile.fleeWeight * fleeScale

  separation = engine.separate(body, body.index, old,
    threshold = separationThreshold, falloff = linear)
  cohesion = zero when neighbours is empty, otherwise
    engine.arrive(body, centre, slowRadius, targetRadius = 0, responseTime)
  alignment = zero when neighbours is empty, otherwise
    engine.matchVelocity(body, meanVelocity, responseTime)

  angle = wanderAmplitude * engine.sine(wanderRate * seconds) * body.wanderSign
  wandering = engine.wander(body with wanderAngle = angle,
    wanderOffset, wanderRadius, responseTime)
  fleeing = engine.flee(body, player)

  acceleration = engine.blend([
    (separationWeight, separation), (cohesionWeight, cohesion),
    (alignmentWeight, alignment), (wanderWeight, wandering),
    (fleeWeight, fleeing)
  ], maxAcceleration)

  nextVelocity = clipLength(body.velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
  next[body] = body with velocity = nextVelocity,
    position = body.position + nextVelocity * timeStep,
    heading = direction(nextVelocity) when moving, otherwise body.heading
creatures = next

item0.project: Sheep_Dog_Game · sheep controller and boids force
item0.relevance: Sheep_Dog_Game is a Python/Pygame herding game. Its sheep are assembled from flocking, threat responses and state-specific movement, making the controller useful to read as a complete game creature.
item0.explanation: compute_boids_force weights separation, alignment and cohesion together with distance-faded dog and owner repulsion and a wolf-panic term. Sheep.update changes that force for grazing, alert, herded and fleeing states; grazing adds a wandering target and herded movement biases towards the pen. It adds remembered threats, whistle recall, boundary repulsion and terrain avoidance around the steering. A penned sheep stops, so reaching the game's goal changes the creature's controller.

limits.item0: Player response currently has scale {fleeScale}. With that response switched off, all social and wander rules remain but the creatures cannot react to Kit; this can let him approach Fern much more closely. Flocking alone does not supply the interaction that a herding game promises.
limits.item1: Blending gives flee no guaranteed precedence over cohesion or wander. It also cannot produce an away direction when Kit and Fern occupy exactly the same point: engine flee returns no acceleration there. Such a contact needs a separate collision or arbitration rule.
limits.item2: Flee means away from Kit, not towards a game objective. Place Kit on the other side of the same herd and the flee contribution reverses. A controller for the player, an explicit goal or a higher-level creature state must supply the intended drive.
limits.item3: Cohesion and alignment lose their targets when a creature has no nearby member of its own species. A goat cannot regroup with sheep under this perception policy. Retaining a herd target or changing membership is a separate design decision.
limits.item4: The prescribed wander wobble and fixed profiles have no memory, grazing state or concept of being safely penned. The opened herding implementation adds those decisions and world avoidance explicitly; this study stops at the steering composition that those decisions can select.

item2.why: Reach for Flee when the task is simply to respond to the player's position, including the missing direction at exact coincidence.

item3.why: Read Weighted blending when choosing a species profile exposes cancellation, scaling or acceleration-limit problems.

item4.why: Choose Priority steering when a threat or collision response should take precedence over ordinary social movement.

intuition.text: A stop command does not erase momentum. The loading-bay cart can receive a strong braking request while its motor removes speed much more slowly. Looking at the request and the motion together exposes the gap between a controller's intention and the body that must carry it out.
intuition.situation: A rail cart must halt before a painted safety line. Its steering controller already wants it stationary; the question is whether the available brake can make that happen within the remaining rail.

example.name: The loading-bay rail cart
example.description: The cart begins at the origin travelling at {initialSpeed} units/s, with the safety line at {stopLine} units. It asks for zero velocity over a response time of {responseTime} s. The steering request has an acceleration limit of {steeringLimit} units/s², while the motor can brake at only {motorBrake} units/s². The run advances by {timeStep} s for {duration} s. This study calls the scene engine's matchVelocity for the request; the straight-rail brake policy and fixed-step integration are study-local, because the public engine has no separate motor-control adapter.

step0.title: Ask the steering controller to stop
step0.text: The velocity goal is zero. The engine's matchVelocity divides the velocity gap by {responseTime} s, then clips the acceleration vector to the steering limit. At this moment it requests {requested} units/s². This is a request to the motor, not a replacement for the current speed.

step1.title: Apply the brake the cart actually has
step1.text: The rail cart accepts only braking between the negative motor limit and zero. Its study-local adapter applies {applied} units/s². A larger request cannot create extra brake capacity; it stays saturated until the velocity gap becomes small enough.

step2.title: Change speed before moving the body
step2.text: Applied acceleration changes speed over the fixed step. Clamp speed at zero because this brake cannot propel the cart backwards, then move using the updated speed. The safety line is only a marker: remaining clearance is {remaining} units, and there is no wall clamp to hide a crossing.

pseudocode.ordinary:
requested = engine.matchVelocity(body, zeroVelocity, responseTime)
// body.maxAcceleration is the steering limit

applied = max(-motorBrake, min(0, requested.x))

velocity = max(0, velocity + applied * timeStep)
position = position + velocity * timeStep

item0.relevance: gdx-ai's Box2D test entity connects steering behaviours to a physics body. It is a concrete example of the boundary where a movement request must become body motion.
item0.explanation: Its update calculates steering output and passes that output to applySteering. The adapter applies linear output as force at the body's centre and angular output as torque when facing is independent; otherwise it aligns facing to velocity. It also attempts speed caps. The file flags a timing problem with those caps, and its comment proposes an additional motor filter for vehicle constraints without implementing that filter. The physics adapter is real; a car-specific motor model is left to its caller.

limits.item0: Limiting a request makes the response feasible, but does not guarantee a safe stopping distance. The comparison changes only brake capacity to {weakBrake} units/s² and exposes whether the cart passes the same safety line.
limits.item1: The brake is a scalar cap for a point moving on a straight rail. It does not model wheel slip, changing load, turning geometry or an animation controller; those require a motor model with the corresponding capabilities.
limits.item2: A fixed-step update is part of this example's contract. Its zero-speed clamp prevents brake-driven reversal; it is not a controller for deliberately reversing the cart, and it never snaps the cart to the safety line.

intuition.text: A beacon above an atrium can share its ground coordinates with a drone that is still far below it. Height must participate in the steering calculation and in the success check. The nose also needs an elevation as well as a compass direction, while rolling the wings remains a separate choice.
intuition.situation: An inspection drone approaches a maintenance beacon in open air. A ground-plane adapter can put its shadow in the right place without putting the drone at the beacon.

example.name: The atrium inspection drone
example.description: The drone starts at rest and approaches the beacon at ({targetX}, {targetY}, {targetZ}), with y meaning height and z depth. It has total speed limit {maxSpeed} units/s, acceleration limit {maxAcceleration} units/s² and fixed steps of {timeStep} s. Its nose immediately follows velocity; roll is the independent {roll}° inspection pose. The last partial step is clamped to the target, which makes this a representation study rather than a braking or aircraft simulation.

step0.title: Keep the height component in the request
step0.text: Subtract the full position from the beacon position, normalise that offset and multiply by the acceleration limit. The volume normalisation shares one acceleration budget across all axes. This step is local: the public scene engine exports planar Vec2 steering, so passing its Seek an extra height property would not create volume steering. The comparison changes only the height weight from {verticalWeight} to {flatVerticalWeight}.

step1.title: Integrate a bounded velocity in the volume
step1.text: Add acceleration multiplied by the step time, then cap the length of the complete velocity vector at {maxSpeed} units/s. Move using that capped velocity. On this straight approach, clamp the last partial step to the effective target and stop; that explicit teaching rule avoids repeated passes through the beacon and provides no physical braking guarantee.

step2.title: Specify the pose as well as the direction
step2.text: Yaw comes from velocity in x/z; pitch comes from its height component relative to horizontal speed. Retain the last direction when stopped, and keep the previous yaw for a purely vertical direction. The roll command rotates the wing about the nose without changing the flight path. Local pose construction uses the public engine’s deterministic sine and cosine, then projects the nose, wing and height connector onto the motion drawing.

pseudocode.ordinary:
effectiveTarget = beacon
effectiveTarget.y = position.y + verticalWeight * (beacon.y - position.y)
offset = effectiveTarget - position
acceleration = length3(offset) == 0 ? zero3
  : offset * maxAcceleration / length3(offset)  // local volume Seek

candidateVelocity = capLength3(velocity + acceleration * dt, maxSpeed)
nextVelocity = candidateVelocity
travel = candidateVelocity * dt
if length3(travel) >= length3(offset):
  nextPosition = effectiveTarget; nextVelocity = zero3
else:
  nextPosition = position + travel

if horizontalLength(candidateVelocity) > 0:
  yaw = atan2(candidateVelocity.z, candidateVelocity.x)
if length3(candidateVelocity) > 0:
  pitch = atan2(candidateVelocity.y, horizontalLength(candidateVelocity))
roll = rollCommand
pose = localForwardAndRolledWing(yaw, pitch, roll)
project(nextPosition, pose, groundProjection)  // drawing only

visual.textEquivalent: At {seconds} s the drone is at ({x}, {y}, {z}), {distance} units from the beacon, moving at {speed} units/s; its nose has yaw {yaw}° and pitch {pitch}°, and its wing has independent roll {roll}° above a ground projection at height {groundHeight}.

item0.relevance: Yuka is a JavaScript game-AI library whose vehicle and steering types work with Vector3. It provides a public example of steering operating in a volume.
item0.explanation: SeekBehavior constructs a maximum-speed desired velocity towards a Vector3 target and returns its difference from current velocity. Vehicle asks its steering manager for force, divides by mass, integrates velocity, caps total speed and updates position. It can turn towards the next position, or use a smoothed velocity for orientation. The smoothing changes orientation rather than the integrated position.

limits.item0: Discarding the height offset can make the drone stop beneath the beacon. The comparison measures full spatial distance, so a successful ground projection cannot conceal the remaining height gap.
limits.item1: Immediate yaw and pitch changes plus a final-step stop do not respect angular acceleration, inertia, braking distance or lift. The commanded roll is an inspection pose, not an aerodynamic rule that generates a turn.
limits.item2: Yaw is undetermined for a purely vertical velocity. This model retains its previous yaw there; a full orientation controller must also decide how to turn smoothly between poses.
limits.item3: Open-air point steering supplies no obstacle volume or swept collision test. Keeping height in the state does not make a route through an atrium roof safe.

item0.why: Use the simpler upright representation for a ground character whose height follows a level or a jump while its facing needs only yaw.

intuition.text: Give the courier a feeler ahead of its travel. A hit supplies more than a warning: the surface normal tells it which way leads back into free space. Put a temporary target along that normal and let the courier pull towards it. The ray can see a wall before the courier’s body reaches it, but detection still needs time to change motion.
intuition.situation: A courier approaches the end of a depot courtyard wall on the way to an offset delivery point. Compare its path with the same run using a ray too short to hit. The difference reveals how much of the turn comes from avoidance and how much comes from seeking the delivery.

example.name: Courier at the depot courtyard wall
example.description: The courier starts at ({startX}, {startY}) with velocity ({velocityX}, {velocityY}) units/s and radius {radius}. Its delivery point is ({goalX}, {goalY}); a vertical wall runs from ({wallX}, {wallBottom}) to ({wallX}, {wallTop}). A forward ray of length {rayLength} units constructs an avoidance target {avoidDistance} units along the hit normal. Maximum speed is {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration {maxAcceleration} units/s². The run takes {steps} fixed steps of {timeStep} s. Segment intersection and target selection are study-local; the actual pull to either target calls engine Seek.

step0.title: Cast a finite forward ray
step0.text: Normalise the current velocity and extend it by {rayLength}; at zero speed retain the last travel heading. The local detector intersects this finite segment with the finite wall segment using cross products. Both intersection fractions must lie within the segments. It reports the actual hit point and a unit surface normal facing against the incoming ray. Parallel and collinear segments return no hit in this small detector.

step1.title: Build a target from the hit normal
step1.text: A hit replaces the delivery point with hitPoint + normal × {avoidDistance}. The offset is a centre-target distance, not an automatic guarantee about the courier’s radius. The normal arrow ends at the avoidance cross. Without a hit the selected target is the delivery point, so local avoidance has no memory of the blocked route.

step2.title: Pull with engine Seek
step2.text: The model passes the selected target to the existing engine Seek function. It returns acceleration towards that target, capped at {maxAcceleration}. When the target still lies ahead, a ray hit can initially leave the pull pointing towards the wall; once the courier passes the offset target the pull points back. Detection alone never sets the courier’s velocity to zero.

step3.title: Measure body clearance and advance
step3.text: Find the nearest point on the finite wall segment and subtract {radius} from its distance to the courier’s centre. This body clearance stays meaningful beside the wall and round either end; a negative value means overlap. Add acceleration times {timeStep} to velocity, clip speed to {maxSpeed}, then advance position. The local update applies no wall clamp or collision response.

pseudocode.ordinary:
direction = normalise(velocity) if moving else lastTravelHeading
rayEnd = position + direction * rayLength
hit = intersectFiniteSegments(position, rayEnd, wallStart, wallEnd)
// Accept only intersection fractions in [0, 1]; normal opposes the ray.

if hit exists: target = hit.point + hit.normal * avoidDistance
else: target = deliveryPoint

acceleration = sceneEngine.seek(body, target)
// Seek pulls towards the selected point; it does not command a stop.

nearestWallPoint = (wallX, clamp(position.y, wallBottom, wallTop))
bodyClearance = distance(position, nearestWallPoint) - radius
velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * dt, maxSpeed)
position += velocity * dt
if moving: lastTravelHeading = normalise(velocity)

visual.textEquivalent: At {seconds} s the courier is at {position} with radius {radius}, velocity {velocity} units/s and acceleration {acceleration} units/s²; its ray runs from {rayStart} to {rayEnd} against the wall from {wallStart} to {wallEnd}, with {rayStatus}, normal {normal}, avoidance target {avoidanceTarget} and selected target {selectedTarget}; delivery remains at {goal}, and body clearance from the finite wall is {clearance} units: {decision}

item0.relevance: gdx-ai’s Java steering library separates ray configurations, collision detectors and obstacle-avoidance steering.
item0.explanation: Version 1.8.2 updates its configured rays, asks the detector for each hit and retains the nearest hit to the owner. It constructs a target using the hit normal multiplied by the owner’s bounding radius plus distanceFromBoundary, then normalises the offset to maximum acceleration. No hit produces zero steering, so another behaviour must supply travel. The source discusses corner trapping and alternative ray configurations.

item0.title: AI for Games, third edition · Chapter 3 Movement, §3.3.15 Obstacle and Wall Avoidance
item0.supports: The book covers this topic at Chapter 3, §3.3.15; no claim is made about its unread text.

item1.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · RaycastObstacleAvoidance.java
item1.supports: Configurable rays, nearest-hit selection, normal-offset target construction and acceleration towards that target; its commentary identifies corner trapping.

limits.item0: A longer ray is not automatically safer. Across the offered lengths from 10 to 12, the greatest body overlap in this setup is {longRayOverlap} units. These rays hit from the start and can pull towards a target still ahead before braking. A shorter ray of length {comparisonRayLength} supplies the comparison; neither length guarantees collision-free motion.
limits.item1: Try the delivery straight ahead at height {comparisonGoalY}: there is no sideways cue. The courier can switch between delivery and avoidance targets while staying on the same line. A ray-based local pull does not choose a route round a wall.
limits.item2: A single centre ray does not sweep the whole disc. It can miss a wall edge that the courier’s radius clips. The local detector also deliberately returns no collision for parallel or collinear segments.
limits.item3: Several rays can alternate between adjacent faces at a corner and keep reversing the chosen target. That is the Corner trap; this straight-wall example does not implement a remedy for it.

item0.why: Reach for Corner trap when adjacent faces make ray-selected targets alternate and the character cannot free itself.

item1.why: Ray configurations is the next choice when one centre feeler misses edges or needs side coverage in a passage.

item2.why: The Collision detector interface separates geometry from steering when several obstacle shapes must provide consistent hit points and normals.

item3.why: Seek is the actual motor used here once a ray hit has supplied a temporary target.

item4.why: Collision avoidance predicts another moving centre’s closest approach; use it for moving characters rather than a static surface normal.

intuition.text: Mica wants to reach the loading bay, but a parked trolley demands room. Adding the two requests could let eagerness weaken braking. Give Clearance ownership of acceleration while it has something to say, then let Travel take over when it declines. Think of ordered handlers returning a result: the winner supplies the whole vector.
intuition.situation: Use this order when Mica must give personal space precedence over progress towards the loading bay. It is useful only if the urgent group becomes quiet when its condition passes.

example.name: Mica approaching a parked trolley
example.description: Mica starts at rest on an aisle with a parked trolley between the courier and the loading bay. Clearance wakes inside {separationThreshold} units and has priority {clearancePriority}: {order}. A request must exceed epsilon {epsilon} units/s² to take control. Speed is limited to {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration to {maxAcceleration} units/s², with decisions every {timeStep} s. The inner ring marks touching centre distance {contactDistance} units. Change the priority, buffer or threshold to see which requests actually move Mica; the comparison reverses only the group order.

step0.title: Measure the trolley before moving
step0.text: Read Mica and the stationary trolley from the current frame. Engine separate measures the centre gap, currently {gap}, and produces a push away inside separationThreshold. This example chooses linear falloff: the push grows with the fraction of that distance still occupied. On the edge and outside it, the push is zero.

step1.title: Build a Clearance group that can decline
step1.text: While separation is nonzero, blend its request with a request to match zero velocity over responseTime. The weights are separationWeight and brakeWeight; engine blend sums and clips them to maxAcceleration. Clearance currently requests {clearanceAcceleration} units/s² along the aisle. When separation is zero, return zero for the whole group: braking must not keep this priority permanently active.

step2.title: Build the Travel group
step2.text: Engine arrive asks for motion towards the loading bay, using slowRadius, targetRadius and responseTime. Its desired speed fades to zero halfway inside targetRadius; its acceleration is clipped to maxAcceleration. Travel currently requests {travelAcceleration} units/s². It remains a complete candidate even when Clearance will win.

step3.title: Let the first substantial request own acceleration
step3.text: Clearance priority {clearancePriority} gives the order {order}. Call engine firstActive: a magnitude must be strictly greater than epsilon, so equality declines. At this moment {activeGroup} supplies {selectedMagnitude} units/s². The losing group contributes nothing. If both decline, firstActive returns zero; ordering the groups chooses a request rather than adding them.

step4.title: Advance and decide again
step4.text: This study uses a local fixed-step integrator: add acceleration × timeStep to velocity, clip speed, then move with the new velocity. The next decision reads the new state. Steering and integration are distinct: zero acceleration preserves momentum here. Touching is measured without a collision response, and there is no automatic rest snap.

pseudocode.ordinary:
body = current Mica state
trolley = stationary body at trolleyPosition
push = engine.separate(body, bodyIndex, [body, trolley],
  { separationThreshold, separationFalloff })

brake = engine.matchVelocity(body, zero, responseTime)
clearance = zero if length(push) == 0 else engine.blend([
  { acceleration: push, weight: separationWeight },
  { acceleration: brake, weight: brakeWeight }
], maxAcceleration)

travel = engine.arrive(body, loadingBay,
  { slowRadius, targetRadius, timeToTarget: responseTime })

groups = [clearance, travel] if clearancePriority == 1
         else [travel, clearance]
acceleration = engine.firstActive(groups, epsilon)
// First length strictly above epsilon; zero if neither qualifies.

velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
position = position + velocity * timeStep
// Read these new values on the next update.

visual.textEquivalent: Mica is {gap} units from the trolley, which {trolleyRelationship}. {activeGroup} supplies {selectedMagnitude} units/s² {pushDirection}, with touching starting at {contactDistance} units.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library. PrioritySteering is its reusable controller for giving conditional steering requests precedence over later requests.
item0.explanation: The class evaluates its behaviour list in order and returns as soon as the steering’s squared magnitude exceeds epsilon squared. It records the selected index for inspection. If every result is small, it returns the final behaviour’s result; an empty list returns zero. Behaviours can themselves be blended groups.

item0.title: AI for Games, third edition · Chapter 3 Movement · §3.4 Combining Steering Behaviors · §3.4.3 Priorities
item0.supports: The book covers priority steering in Chapter 3 Movement, §3.4.3 Priorities within §3.4 Combining Steering Behaviors.

item1.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · PrioritySteering.java
item1.supports: An ordered behaviour list uses a strict squared-magnitude threshold, exposes the selected index and retains the last small result when none exceeds the threshold.

limits.item0: With {order}, the minimum gap is {minimumGap} units and there are {touchingSamples} sampled touching moments. Reversing only the order to {comparisonOrder} gives a minimum of {comparisonMinimumGap} units and {comparisonTouchingSamples} touching moments. {outcome} A clearance request can lose when Travel gets first refusal, and a large epsilon can silence both groups.
limits.item1: A crowd under priority steering keeps a faint shimmer in the soldier scene, as docs/dev-reference/architecture/scene.md records. Mica changes selected group {switches} times in the chosen run. A threshold and smooth component forces do not promise a final rest.
limits.item2: Priority does not plan a detour around the trolley. Passing through it in this teaching integrator is an overlap, not a discovered route to the loading bay.
limits.item3: Separation reacts to the current gap. A small clearance distance can leave too little room to brake; a large time step can miss a useful decision or a brief overlap. This integrator measures touching without predictive collision avoidance or rigid body contact handling.

item0.why: Use weighted blending when Mica should compromise between requests within the same priority group; it also explains the sum inside Clearance.

item1.why: Read blending versus arbitration when deciding whether competing requests should share acceleration or one should own it, as Clearance does here.

item2.why: Read separation to change how the trolley’s proximity produces a push, rather than changing which group gets precedence.

item3.why: Use equilibrium fallback when a blended group goes quiet because requests cancel and a later request should move Mica out of that balance.

item4.why: Reach for a steering pipeline when Mica needs coordinated targets and constraints to negotiate the blocked route to the loading bay.

intuition.text: A flare's last visible preview point is not necessarily where it lands. First ask when its height meets the surface; then use that same time to find its horizontal position. At the top of the arc its vertical velocity vanishes, but it still travels sideways. The launch has already determined its flight; nothing is steering it towards the cross.
intuition.situation: A harbour watchkeeper wants to place a marker where a signal flare from the dock roof will meet the water, before releasing it.

example.name: The dock-roof signal flare
example.description: The flare leaves the dock roof at height {launchHeight} m with horizontal velocity {horizontalSpeed} m/s and upward velocity {verticalSpeed} m/s. Gravity is {gravity} m/s² and the selected landing height is {landingHeight} m. Samples are {timeStep} s apart, but the predicted encounter is {landingResult}. The comparison changes only the selected height to {unreachableHeight} m.

step0.title: Give the two axes one clock
step0.text: Use metres, seconds and positive height upwards. Horizontal velocity stays constant; gravity reduces vertical velocity. The scene engine has no projectile predictor, so this study evaluates the constant-gravity equations locally. The drawing reverses height only when converting it to screen coordinates.

step1.title: Solve the height encounter before the range
step1.text: Set height(t) equal to the selected height and form D. The current D is {discriminant}. A negative D means the requested height is never reached. Otherwise take the later nonnegative root: it is the descent encounter, or a touch at the apex. A negative later root means both encounters were in the past. Multiply the accepted time by horizontal velocity to locate the cross.

step2.title: Evaluate the flight at a selected time
step2.text: Use the same t in both position equations and in vertical velocity. At this moment the flare is at horizontal position {x} m and height {height} m, with vertical velocity {verticalVelocity} m/s. The height chart and the drawing read these same calculated states; the arrow shows velocity multiplied by the sample interval.

step3.title: End at the event, not at a convenient sample
step3.text: If the next preview sample would pass contact, evaluate the exact root instead and finish there. The selected surface absorbs the flare, so velocity becomes zero after contact. With no future encounter, show only the bounded free-flight preview and no landing cross. Raising the requested height above the {apexHeight} m apex must produce no landing, rather than a guessed point.

pseudocode.ordinary:
require gravity > 0
use x rightwards and height upwards
horizontalVelocity = launchHorizontalVelocity
verticalAcceleration = -gravity

D = launchVerticalVelocity² + 2 * gravity * (launchHeight - selectedHeight)
landingTime = none
if D >= 0:
  laterRoot = (launchVerticalVelocity + sqrt(D)) / gravity
  if laterRoot >= 0: landingTime = laterRoot
landingX = startX + horizontalVelocity * landingTime, when it exists

for previewTime = 0, dt, 2*dt, ... horizon:
  t = min(previewTime, landingTime), when a landing exists
  x = startX + horizontalVelocity * t
  height = launchHeight + launchVerticalVelocity*t - gravity*t²/2
  verticalVelocity = launchVerticalVelocity - gravity*t
  record the state at t

  if landingTime exists and previewTime >= landingTime:
    set height to selectedHeight and velocity to zero after contact
    end the preview at landingTime
without a future encounter, draw no landing cross

limits.item0: A requested height above the flare's apex has no real encounter time. The comparison exposes this failure; a square root of a negative value is not a landing prediction.
limits.item1: A height encounter is only a candidate landing. This model treats the selected height as an unlimited absorbing plane and does not test the extent of a platform, a wall on the way, or an earlier collision. A raised height can also be crossed on ascent; the later root deliberately selects descent.
limits.item2: The equations assume constant gravity and no air resistance, wind or lift. An accurate root for those assumptions can still disagree with a game that applies drag or a different numerical update.
limits.item3: The preview has a finite time limit. A final preview sample is not proof of contact; a known landing can lie beyond that limit.

intuition.text: Ash wants to tag Reed, who is running along the quay. Steering at Reed's current position aims behind a moving runner. Ash instead aims at a temporary mark ahead of Reed. Each update replaces that mark using the latest motion; it is a forecast that can be revised, rather than a promised meeting place.
intuition.situation: A tagger approaching a runner from the side needs a lead on steady motion. Short predictions near the runner keep the aim responsive, while a cap limits how far into an uncertain future the tagger commits.

example.name: Ash chases Reed on the quay
example.description: Ash approaches Reed’s running line from the side and predicts no more than {maxPrediction} s ahead. Reed runs steadily in the main run; the comparison brings a reversal into that forecast. The ring marks tag range, and entering it measures contact without stopping either runner. Ash observes current motion, never the reversal schedule.

step0.title: Sample the runners now
step0.text: Measure the separation between Ash and Reed, {distance} units, and Ash's actual speed, {speed} units/s. This estimate uses Ash's current speed, not the speed cap or the relative closing speed. It does not solve the interception equation.

step1.title: Choose a bounded lookahead
step1.text: If Ash is stationary, use maxPrediction to avoid dividing by zero. Otherwise use the smaller of maxPrediction and distance / speed. The selected horizon is {prediction} s here. Recomputing it lets the lead shorten as Ash closes in; timeStep still advances only one update.

step2.title: Project Reed and delegate to Seek
step2.text: Project Reed’s current velocity over the chosen horizon to put Aim {leadDistance} units ahead. The engine has no pursuit function: this study calculates that prediction locally, then calls the engine’s seek for {accelerationMagnitude} units/s² of acceleration towards the cross.

step3.title: Advance and observe again
step3.text: Update Ash's velocity with acceleration times timeStep, clip its length to maxSpeed, then move with the updated velocity. Read Reed's scripted position and current velocity at the next sample. The script drives the example only; the predictor sees no future turn. Tag range is a measurement, not an arrival or braking condition.

pseudocode.ordinary:
distance = length(reed.position - ash.position)
speed = length(ash.velocity)

if speed == 0:
  prediction = maxPrediction
else:
  prediction = min(maxPrediction, distance / speed)

predicted = reed.position + reed.velocity * prediction
acceleration = sceneEngine.seek(ash, predicted)

velocity = clipLength(ash.velocity + acceleration * timeStep,
                      ash.maxSpeed)
ash = ash with { position: ash.position + velocity * timeStep, velocity }
seconds = seconds + timeStep
reed = sampleScriptedRunner(seconds)
// Repeat; only current Reed data enters the prediction.

visual.textEquivalent: The Aim cross lies {leadDistance} units ahead of Reed along the runner’s current direction, using a {prediction} s lookahead. Ash is {distance} units from Reed and {closingRelation}, with the pull aimed at the cross.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library whose generic Pursue behaviour accepts a moving steerable target. It exposes a prediction cap for reusable pursuit and evasion steering.
item0.explanation: The code divides squared separation by the owner's squared current speed and takes the square root when that result fits within the cap. At rest it keeps the cap. It projects the target with its current linear velocity, then normalises the offset and scales it to the acceleration limit. An overridable acceleration method lets Evade reverse that output. Despite a comment discussing maximum speed, the calculation reads current velocity.

limits.item0: Reed can reverse after Ash samples the velocity. In the comparison, forecasts made before the reversal miss Reed's actual position at their chosen future time. The error chart measures that miss, not separation between the runners. Replanning corrects subsequent forecasts but cannot undo motion already taken towards an old aim.
limits.item1: The horizon is a heuristic. It ignores Ash's acceleration time and the runners' relative direction, so its value is not an interception deadline. A faster pursuer and an accurate straight-line forecast still do not guarantee an exact meeting.
limits.item2: The closest pass with the selected prediction cap is {closestPass} units. {tagOutcome} Delegating to Seek adds no brake, contact latch or velocity matching; a game rule must finish a tag, or velocity matching can keep Ash beside Reed.
limits.item3: Neither the prediction nor Seek checks whether the route to the amber cross is traversable. A quay wall would need a route or an avoidance rule. A longer horizon also cannot make an unreachable faster runner catchable.

item0.why: Use Seek directly when Reed is stationary or when leading the motion is unnecessary. It is also the acceleration step used after this predictor chooses an aim.

item1.why: Read Prediction time when choosing how far to lead Reed: the cap trades a longer lead against greater exposure to an unseen turn.

item2.why: Use Velocity matching after closing in when Ash should run alongside Reed. Continuing to seek the projected point does not match their velocities.

item3.why: Use Evade when Reed is a pursuer to escape from: the forecast can still supply a future point, but the steering heads away from it.

intuition.text: The shelf runner can be close enough to collect a parcel without standing exactly on a painted cross. Making that acceptable region explicit turns arrival into a decision the task can actually satisfy. It also makes the cost visible: a larger region permits a less precise stop.
intuition.situation: A shelf runner advances in fixed strides towards a pickup marker that falls between the positions those strides can reach.

example.name: The shelf runner accepts a pickup region
example.description: The runner starts at {start}; the pickup marker is at {target}. Outside a satisfaction radius of {satisfactionRadius} units, it moves towards the marker at {speed} units/s for each {timeStep} s update, a stride of {stride} units. The accepted interval runs from {lowerEdge} to {upperEdge}, including both edges. The run contains {steps} updates. The tolerance check and direct movement are study-local: the public scene engine exposes acceleration steering rather than this constant-stride controller.

step0.title: Measure distance before moving
step0.text: The runner compares its current sampled position with the marker. The signed offset selects a direction if movement is needed; its magnitude, currently {distance} units, decides acceptance. The radius is a positional tolerance, not the runner body size.

step1.title: Accept the interval, including its boundary
step1.text: If distance is at or below {satisfactionRadius} units, set velocity to zero and keep the present position. At this moment the decision is {accepted}. No snap is added: a successful decision may leave a visible gap to the cross.

step2.title: Take a full stride only outside
step2.text: If the check fails, assign the signed travel speed and advance by velocity × {timeStep} s. The assigned velocity is {velocity} units/s and the next position is {nextPosition}. There is no speed taper, inertia or between-sample intersection test in this controller.

visual.textEquivalent: The shelf runner is at {position}, {distance} units from the pickup cross at {target}, with an accepted circle of radius {satisfactionRadius} and an accepted aisle interval from {lowerEdge} to {upperEdge}; it is {accepted}, assigns velocity {velocity} units/s and its next sampled position is {nextPosition}.

item0.project: highnet · AI Steering Behaviors for Games
item0.relevance: This public Unity C# project supplies movement components. Its KinematicArrive component is useful here because its translation coroutine has an explicit target-radius decision.
item0.explanation: The coroutine normalises the target direction and translates by maxSpeed only when distance is at least targetRadius. It waits translationWaitSeconds between decisions, but does not multiply the translation by elapsed time. Its strict accepted region excludes equality, and the translation has no speed taper. The class name alone therefore does not imply proportional slowing.

item1.relevance: gdx-ai is a reusable Java game-AI library. Its Arrive behaviour exposes arrivalTolerance separately from the radius that begins deceleration.
item1.explanation: The arrivalTolerance check uses distance at or below the threshold to return zero steering acceleration. Outside it, the routine calculates a target velocity, then a bounded acceleration from the velocity gap. The routine does not set the owner velocity to zero, so the caller still owns the integration and stopping policy.

limits.item0: Changing only the radius to {comparisonRadius} units demands an exact sampled landing. With this marker and stride, the runner alternates across the cross and never accepts a position. The comparison chart makes those reversals visible.
limits.item1: A band narrower than the gap between reachable samples may be crossed entirely between updates. This controller checks endpoints only, so crossing the band is insufficient; reduce the stride, taper movement or add an intersection policy when that matters.
limits.item2: A radius large enough to include the starting place reports success before the runner travels. Choose the permitted placement error from the pickup task rather than widening it until jitter disappears.
limits.item3: A satisfaction decision does not provide braking. This runner can set velocity to zero immediately; a physical character needs a speed condition or a braking controller as well as a position tolerance.

item1.why: Use Arrive when the runner has momentum and needs acceleration to slow before a positional tolerance can count as a settled stop.

item2.why: Use Slow radius and target radius when separating the place where braking begins from the place accepted as reached.

intuition.text: At the Lantern Gate muster, another scout should extend the patrol's wedge without requiring a newly drawn template. Treat the layout as a calculation from member count and spacing. That calculation can accommodate everyone and still produce a group too wide for the lane: accepting a count is not evidence that the result fits its surroundings.
intuition.situation: A patrol planner needs a recognisable wedge as scouts join. A preview can regenerate the destinations and check the resulting footprint before issuing any movement orders.

example.name: The Lantern Gate muster
example.description: The Lantern Gate patrol grows from {initialCount} to {targetCount} scouts on a regular joining schedule, using spacing {spacing} units in a {laneWidth}-unit lane. The engine generates a centred wedge for each count. Dots sit on proposed target rings, with circles showing body size, while the anchor stays on the lane's centre line. The chart tracks the full transverse footprint. The comparison changes only the requested membership and checks whether either muster outgrows the lane; the preview does not simulate journeys between layouts.

step0.title: Read membership before generating geometry
step0.text: The local schedule adds a scout at the first joining sample and another after each joining interval, stopping at {targetCount} members. At {seconds} seconds there are {count}. The schedule makes changes easy to inspect; a game would usually receive membership changes from its formation manager.

step1.title: Generate and centre the wedge
step1.text: patternSlots places a tip and alternates slots down the arms, extending a row after each pair. Spacing is {spacing} units along each local axis. The engine subtracts the raw slots' mean so that the anchor stays at the mean slot centre. An incomplete row can move earlier offsets sideways as well as forwards; the worked step shows that recentring.

step2.title: Inspect the proposed positions
step2.text: Add the stationary anchor to each offset to get the proposed destinations. At this sample the largest shift of a retained slot from the preceding proposal is {retainedShift} units. This is a layout change; deciding which scout should walk where and planning that journey are separate tasks.

step3.title: Check the whole footprint against the lane
step3.text: The transverse centre span is {centreSpan} units. Include a body radius of {memberRadius} at both edges: the footprint is {width} units against a lane width of {laneWidth}. The smallest clearance to either edge is {clearance} units: {fitStatus}. Generating more slots does not make the lane wider.

pseudocode.ordinary:
joins = clamp(1 + floor((step - joinStart) / joinInterval),
              0, targetCount - initialCount)
count = initialCount + joins

// The engine alternates slots along the wedge's arms,
// then subtracts the mean of all generated offsets.
offsets = patternSlots("wedge", count, spacing)

positions = offsets.map(offset => anchor + offset)
retainedShift = max(distance(previous[i], positions[i])
                    for each retained slot i)
// Draw positions as proposals; do not integrate any movement.

centreSpan = max(positions.y) - min(positions.y)
width = centreSpan + 2 * memberRadius
upperClearance = min(positions.y) - memberRadius - upperLaneEdge
lowerClearance = lowerLaneEdge - max(positions.y) - memberRadius
clearance = min(upperClearance, lowerClearance)
report(width, clearance >= 0)

visual.textEquivalent: The tip leads arms of proposed scouts around the stationary anchor. The {count}-member wedge is {width} units wide in a {laneWidth}-unit lane, with minimum edge clearance {clearance} units ({fitStatus}).

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library. Its defensive circle is a concrete scalable pattern that accounts for both membership and member size.
item0.explanation: The pattern stores the slot count and sets its radius to memberRadius / sin(pi / count). Slots use evenly spaced angles and face outwards. A lone member is placed at the origin, and supportsSlots accepts every count. The radius calculation keeps neighbouring centres a member diameter apart, so adding members expands the circle rather than adding points to an unchanged circumference.

limits.item0: The selected patrol ends with a footprint of {finalWidth} units in a {laneWidth}-unit lane: {finalFitStatus}. The recipe supplies slots even when they cross the lane edges; choosing a narrower pattern or rejecting the muster requires another planning decision.
limits.item1: Adding a scout can move existing slot targets because the engine centres the newly generated set. Stable slot indices do not guarantee stable destinations; the incomplete-row moment makes that discontinuity visible.
limits.item2: These proposals say where scouts should end up. They do not assign named scouts to destinations or plan their journeys, so they establish no claim about avoiding collisions while the patrol rearranges.

item0.why: Use fixed formations when a settled set of escort offsets should follow a leader. Regenerating a shape for changed membership is a separate concern.

item1.why: Use the formation pattern interface when several layout recipes need the same count, slot-location and capacity contract, including a way to decline unsupported membership.

item2.why: Use slot assignment when the planner must decide which named scout should occupy each generated destination. A list of positions cannot make that choice.

intuition.text: Mica's courier motor always pulls towards a beacon. That sounds like a move order, but the pull changes velocity gradually: it does not replace the velocity Mica already has. A sideways start survives the approach, carries Mica past the beacon and bends the return into an orbit. Watch the green velocity line and the amber acceleration line separate.
intuition.situation: Use this steering primitive when Mica needs a persistent pull towards a destination, such as one contribution to a combined movement rule. A delivery that must finish at the beacon also needs a way to shed speed.

example.name: Mica's courier and the beacon
example.description: Mica starts left of a fixed beacon with sideways speed {startSidewaysSpeed} units/s and an inward acceleration limit of {maxAcceleration} units/s². Set Sideways start to zero to see straight overshoot, then raise it to bend the return into an orbit. The drawing keeps the path; the comparison uses a straight start with the same motor.

step0.title: Locate the beacon from Mica
step0.text: Subtract Mica’s position from the beacon’s position to find the direction of the pull. The remaining distance is {distance} units; this gap says where to accelerate, not how fast Mica is already travelling.

step1.title: Ask the engine for acceleration
step1.text: The engine’s seek normalises the target offset and scales it by maxAcceleration, requesting {accelerationMagnitude} units/s² here. A zero offset produces zero acceleration; otherwise a nearby beacon still requests the full pull.

step2.title: Change velocity and enforce the speed cap
step2.text: Add acceleration multiplied by timeStep to the current velocity. The trial speed is {trialSpeed} units/s; clipLength limits its magnitude to maxSpeed while keeping its direction. A speed cap bounds motion but does not ask for a slower approach.

step3.title: Move with the updated velocity
step3.text: Move for timeStep using that clipped velocity, then measure the beacon again on the next step. This study uses the engine's vector arithmetic and its velocity-before-position update order on an open plane. Nothing snaps Mica onto the beacon or cancels the sideways motion.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library. Its generic Seek behaviour provides an acceleration calculation for steerable owners with a target location.
item0.explanation: The calculation subtracts the owner's position from the target's, normalises the resulting vector and scales it by the active limiter's maximum linear acceleration. It sets angular acceleration to zero and returns the steering output. Target access and a replaceable limiter make this a reusable behaviour; applying that output and enforcing a speed cap belong to the caller.

intuition.text: Mira and Rowan need room at an archive shelf. Each can push away from the other, but that request takes time to change an existing velocity. Asking for space cannot guarantee that their footprints stay apart.
intuition.situation: Use separation when nearby characters should spread out without assigning each a destination. At the shelf, it supplies an outward push; another controller would be needed to tell the couriers where to finish.

example.name: Mira and Rowan making room at the archive shelf
example.description: The same pair is shown twice: inverse-square falloff above, linear falloff below. They begin {initialGap} units apart, each with initial inward speed {inwardSpeed} units/s and neighbour range {threshold} units. Both runs call the scene engine's separate function, then a study-local update changes velocity before position. Outer circles show Mira's neighbourhood; inner circles show both footprints. Change inward speed to inspect overlap, or neighbour range to change when repulsion acts.

step0.title: Read the pair before either courier moves
step0.text: Both couriers read the same positions. Mira ignores herself and only considers Rowan when their centre distance is below {threshold} units. The current inverse-square gap is {squareGap}; the linear run's gap is {linearGap}. Exactly at the threshold there is no push.

step1.title: Choose how the push fades with distance
step1.text: With acceleration limit A, threshold R and body diameter c, linear strength is A × (R − d) / R. Inverse-square strength is min(A, A × c² × (1/d² − 1/R²)); subtracting the value at R makes it reach zero at the boundary too. The current pushes are {squareAcceleration} units/s² above and {linearAcceleration} below, so inverse-square need not mean stronger at every distance.

step2.title: Add vectors, then cap their length
step2.text: Each contribution points away from its neighbour. There is only a single neighbour here, but a crowd adds all such vectors before the final length cap. The engine supplies opposite directions even for coincident positions, using the couriers' list order. Symmetric contributions from different neighbours can still cancel.

step3.title: Apply the push over a fixed interval
step3.text: Update velocity over {timeStep} s, cap speed at {maxSpeed} units/s, then move using that new velocity. Mira's current speed is {squareSpeed} units/s above and {linearSpeed} below. Outside the neighbourhood, zero acceleration preserves velocity: separation supplies no finishing brake.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a reusable Java library for game AI. Its Separation behaviour shows how a steering calculation can receive neighbours through a proximity service rather than searching the whole world itself.
item0.explanation: Separation asks its Proximity object to report neighbours. Each callback computes an outward unit direction, scales it by decayCoefficient / distanceSquared with a per-neighbour acceleration cap, and accumulates the result. Coincident positions are skipped. The class offers a configurable decay coefficient and works with the library's vector abstraction; applying the returned acceleration belongs to the game's movement code.

item1.title: Craig Reynolds · Steering Behaviors For Autonomous Characters · Separation
item1.supports: Separation finds local neighbours and sums outward contributions; distance weighting is a design choice, and spatial partitioning can restrict the neighbour search.

item2.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · Separation.java
item2.supports: The implementation uses a Proximity callback, inverse-square strength, a per-neighbour cap and an explicit skip for coincident positions.

limits.item0: At the comparison speed of {fastInwardSpeed} units/s each, the couriers overlap before repulsion turns them apart. Separation reads present distance, so it cannot reserve the stopping distance that a fast approach needs; the comparison changes only initial inward speed.
limits.item1: Once the couriers leave their {threshold}-unit neighbourhood, the push ends but their outward velocity remains. Add a destination or velocity controller when making room should finish with a stop.
limits.item2: Equal pushes from opposite neighbours can cancel even at an uncomfortably small spacing. The special direction for exact coincidence does not resolve every crowded arrangement.
limits.item3: This pair uses an exhaustive neighbour list. Repeating that search for every courier in a large crowd grows quadratically; a spatial index can reduce the search while preserving the same local force rule.

item0.why: Reach for weighted blending when Mira and Rowan should keep their distance while also heading somewhere; separation alone supplies no destination or brake.

item1.why: Read decay function when choosing how strongly a near neighbour should matter relative to a farther one; the shelf runs expose that choice directly.

item2.why: Use spatial partitioning for neighbours when the shelf becomes a crowd and finding the local couriers costs more than calculating their pushes.

item3.why: Use collision avoidance when closing velocity must influence the decision before the couriers become close; the fast shelf approach needs anticipation.
