intuition.text: Think of observeOn as a hand-off desk between the source and everything after it. The source keeps working at its own pace; what moves is the moment the next stage is told. Name animationFrameScheduler and the news waits for the browser's next paint; asapScheduler, for the code running now to finish; queueScheduler, for a delivery already under way to end. Nothing is merged or reordered at the desk: things are heard in the order they happened, only later.
intuition.situation: An upload's progress bar. The upload reports progress whenever the network does, sometimes twice between two paints of the screen, and its stream is not yours to change. Drawing the bar is only useful just before the browser paints, so you choose when the bar hears a report rather than when the upload makes one.

example.name: An upload that fails, heard at each paint
example.description: The upload reports {reports} at frames 1, 2 and 5, and fails at frame 6 with {failure}. The browser paints every {paintEvery} frames, starting at frame 3. The bar subscribes through observeOn(animationFrameScheduler), so it hears the reports only at a paint, and hears the failure after the last report rather than before it.

step0.title: Hand each notification to the scheduler
step0.text: When the upload reports progress, fails or completes, observeOn does not call the bar. It schedules a task on animationFrameScheduler that will pass that notification on.

step1.title: Wait for the next paint
step1.text: animationFrameScheduler keeps its tasks in a queue. The first task asks the browser for an animation frame; a task that arrives before that frame joins the same queue and asks for nothing more.

step2.title: Deliver the queue in order
step2.text: Just before the browser paints, the scheduler runs every task queued for that frame, oldest first. Reports that arrived between two paints reach the bar together, one after the other, and the screen shows only the last.

step3.title: An error waits its turn
step3.text: The upload's failure is one more task in the queue, so it reaches the bar after the reports before it, at the next paint. The upload's own subscription ended when it failed: observeOn changes when the bar hears, never when the upload runs.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each report, error or completion from the upload:
  schedule a task that passes it to the bar
  (the bar hears nothing yet)

if no animation frame has been requested:
  request the next one from the browser
otherwise:
  the task joins the queue for that frame

when the frame comes, just before the paint:
  run every queued task, oldest first
  (reports that arrived together are heard together)

an error is one more task in the queue:
  the bar hears it after the reports queued before it
  (the upload itself stopped when it failed)

visual.textEquivalent: Frame {frame}: {now}. The bar has heard {delivered}.

item0.relevance: NgRx Store computes its state by passing the stream of dispatched actions through observeOn(queueScheduler) before the reducer, in modules/store/src/state.ts of the ngrx/platform repository.
item0.explanation: The State class pipes the actions through observeOn(queueScheduler), then withLatestFrom(reducer$) and scan, which folds each action into the state. queueScheduler runs a task at once unless another of its tasks is running, in which case the new task waits for that one to finish. So when code that hears a new state dispatches another action straight away, that action is reduced after the current one has been delivered rather than in the middle of it, one action at a time in the order dispatched. This is the author's reading of the pipeline from queueScheduler's documented behaviour; the file does not state its reason. It is the same operator as the study's with another scheduler: the phase it chooses is after the delivery under way, not before the next paint. The file is pinned to tag 22.0.1, read on 2026-10-31.

item0.title: RxJS API reference · observeOn
item0.supports: observeOn reschedules every notification of the source, errors and completion included, on the scheduler it is given, with an optional delay; the source keeps its own scheduler; using it to split a synchronous burst is an anti-pattern, for which the scheduler belongs in the source; delay, unlike observeOn, passes errors on at once; and the page's own example observes an interval on animationFrameScheduler to update an element just before the browser repaints.

item1.title: observeOn.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item1.supports: At the installed version the operator hands each next, complete and error alike to executeSchedule with the same scheduler and delay, so no notification bypasses the scheduler.

item2.title: AnimationFrameAction.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item2.supports: Without a delay a task joins the scheduler's queue and only the first task queued before a frame requests that animation frame, whose flush runs the queue; with a delay above zero the task is scheduled as an ordinary async action instead.

item3.title: RxJS API reference · animationFrameScheduler
item3.supports: animationFrameScheduler runs a task without a delay just before the browser's next repaint and behaves like asyncScheduler when a delay is given.

item4.title: RxJS guide · Scheduler
item4.supports: observeOn places a proxy observer between the source and the final observer that schedules each notification, so with asyncScheduler the values arrive after the synchronous subscribe call has returned; and the scheduler types: queueScheduler as a trampoline in the current event frame, asapScheduler on the microtask queue, asyncScheduler on timers, animationFrameScheduler before the next repaint.

item5.title: RxJS API reference · queueScheduler
item5.supports: queueScheduler runs a task without a delay synchronously, but a task scheduled while another of its tasks is running is queued until that one finishes; the reading of NgRx Store rests on this.

item6.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item6.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share, including a group in parentheses for emissions in one frame, and the animate run helper, whose marbles mark the paints at which queued animation-frame callbacks run, as the repaint line does here.

limits.item0: observeOn delivers every report; it merges none. Reports that arrive between two paints all reach the bar in one frame, so the bar is drawn more than once and only the last drawing is seen. When only the newest value per frame matters, auditTime(0, animationFrameScheduler) keeps just that one, but it treats the error differently: audit passes an error on the moment it arrives, so on this upload the failure would reach the bar before the next paint and the report waiting for that paint would never be drawn.
limits.item1: It cannot pace a synchronous burst. Had the upload produced all of {reports} at once, observeOn would queue them all before the first paint and deliver them together in it. Spreading them one per paint needs the scheduler inside the source, as scheduled(reports, animationFrameScheduler) does; observeOn only makes deliveries later, never further apart.
limits.item2: It changes when the bar hears, not when the upload runs. The upload's work, its timers and any side effect inside it keep the source's own timing and scheduler; only the hand-off downstream moves. To move the moment the source is subscribed, use subscribeOn instead.
limits.item3: A delay changes the scheduler's character. With a delay above zero, animationFrameScheduler schedules each task on a timer, as asyncScheduler would, so delivery no longer waits for a paint and every notification, the error included, is simply held that long. To shift values later, RxJS recommends delay; observeOn is for choosing the scheduler that delivers.
limits.item4: Unsubscribing cancels what is still queued. Each scheduled task belongs to the bar's subscription, so a bar torn down between a report and the next paint never hears that report.
limits.item5: A marble diagram shows the move only when the scheduler moves time. With asapScheduler, or asyncScheduler without a delay, the delivery lands in the same virtual frame as the report, so the marbles match the source's exactly although the bar hears only after the code that subscribed has finished. That order needs an ordinary asynchronous test, which is why this example uses animation frames.

item0.why: subscribeOn moves the subscription itself, so the source starts later; observeOn leaves the start alone and moves each delivery.

item1.why: delay is the tool for shifting values later in time; it passes an error on at once, where observeOn holds the error behind the values before it.

item2.why: auditTime with animationFrameScheduler keeps only the newest value per frame, where observeOn delivers every one.

item3.why: scheduled puts the scheduler inside the source, which is how a synchronous burst is spread over frames; observeOn cannot do that.

item4.why: animationFrameScheduler is the scheduler this example names: a task without a delay runs just before the next repaint, and one frame serves every task queued before it.

item5.why: queueScheduler is the scheduler NgRx Store pairs with observeOn: a task scheduled while another runs waits for it to finish.

item6.why: The rendering pattern this example follows, with auditTime as its alternative when only the last value per frame counts.

notes.0: The upload starts and the bar subscribes through observeOn. Nothing has been reported yet.
notes.1: The upload reports 10%. observeOn does not pass it on: it hands the report to animationFrameScheduler, which asks the browser for the next animation frame.
notes.2: The upload reports 30%. A frame is already requested, so the scheduler only queues this report behind the first. The bar has heard nothing.
notes.3: The browser is about to paint and runs the animation frame. The scheduler delivers both queued reports in order: the bar is drawn at 10% and at once at 30%, and only 30% reaches the screen.
notes.4: Nothing new happens. The queue is empty, and the bar shows 30% until the next report is delivered.
notes.5: The upload reports 60%. The queue is empty again, so the scheduler queues this report and requests a new frame.
notes.6: The connection is lost and the upload errors. Its subscription ends here, but observeOn schedules the error like any other notification, behind 60%.
notes.7: The browser paints again. The bar hears 60% and then the error, in the order they happened, in the same frame.

example.caption: Time runs in frames. progress$ is what the upload reports; repaint is not a stream the pipeline reads but marks each frame at which the browser is about to paint, when animationFrameScheduler runs what it holds; bar$ is what the progress bar hears. A circle is an emission, with its letter; a cross on progress$ or bar$ is the upload failing. bar$’s values do not ride down at a paint: each left progress$ frames earlier and waited in the scheduler’s queue. Step the frames to follow each report from the upload to the bar.

intuition.text: repeat starts a finished stream over. When the source completes, repeat does not pass the completion on: it subscribes to the source again, so whatever the source does on subscription, such as sending a request, happens again. It does this a set number of times or without end, and it can wait between runs.
intuition.situation: A page waiting for a build asks the server for the build's status, waits after each answer and asks again, so the page follows the build from queued to passed without anyone pressing refresh.

example.name: A build's status, asked three times
example.description: The page reads the build's status through check$, which is cold: each subscription sends a new request, whose answer arrives {answerAfter} frames later, and then the request completes. repeat asks {checks} times and waits {wait} frames after each finished check before asking again. The answers are {answers}.

step0.title: Start the check
step0.text: When the page subscribes to status$, repeat subscribes to check$, which sends the first request, and starts counting finished runs from none.

step1.title: Pass on what the run delivers
step1.text: Each answer goes straight to the output, unchanged. An error goes straight through as well and ends the output there: repeat starts over only after a completion, never after a failure.

step2.title: Hold back the completion and count it
step2.text: When a run completes, the output does not. repeat counts the finished run, and once the count reaches {checks} it completes the output instead of going on.

step3.title: Wait, then start the check again
step3.text: Otherwise repeat starts a timer for its delay, {wait} frames here. When the timer fires it subscribes to the source again, which sends a new request, and the next run begins.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the page starts listening:
  finished = 0
  start the check

on each answer from the check:
  pass it to the page
if the check fails:
  pass the failure to the page and stop there

when the check finishes:
  finished = finished + 1
  if finished = count:
    tell the page there are no more answers

  otherwise:
    wait for the delay
    then start the check again

visual.textEquivalent: Frame {frame}: {now}. Answers so far: {delivered}.

item0.title: RxJS API reference · repeat
item0.supports: On the source's completion repeat subscribes to it again; called with nothing it never stops, a count of zero gives an empty result, the delay may be milliseconds or a function of the repetition count, and errors are left to retry.

item1.title: RxJS API reference · RepeatConfig
item1.supports: count is unlimited when left out; delay is either a number of milliseconds or a function that is given the subscription count and returns the notifier to wait for, and a notifier that ends without a value ends the result.

item2.title: repeat.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item2.supports: At the installed version the operator increments its count of finished runs before calling a delay function with it, waits on timer(delay) for a number, resubscribes only from its completion handler and gives the source no error handler of its own, and returns EMPTY without subscribing for a count of zero or less.

item3.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item3.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share, a dash for a frame, a letter for an emission, a bar for completion and a caret and an exclamation mark for the start and end of a subscription, and run mode's virtual time of one millisecond a frame, which makes the example's delay count in frames.

limits.item0: repeat starts over only after a completion. An error goes straight through and ends status$ with no new run; to try again after a failure, reach for retry, the same loop for errors.
limits.item1: A fixed count rarely fits a real poll, which should stop when the answer says so. Put takeWhile after repeat, so that the passed answer completes the output and unsubscribes the loop before another request goes out, or have a delay function return EMPTY, which completes the output instead of repeating.
limits.item2: repeat repeats only what the source does on subscription. A promise-based call made before the pipe, as in from(fetch(url)), is made once, and every repetition reads the same settled answer; wrap the call in defer so that each subscription makes it again. A hot source that has completed completes again at once, so repeating it asks for nothing new.
limits.item3: Over a source that completes as soon as it is subscribed, such as of(...), with no delay, each run starts inside the one before it. A long or endless repeat then runs out of call stack, and the output either fails with a RangeError or simply stops, neither completing nor failing. A timer delay starts each run afresh; a small count, or a take downstream, ends the loop first.
limits.item4: Each wait starts when a run completes, so the time between requests is the answer's time plus the delay, and a fixed delay never backs off: a slow or struggling server is asked as often as ever. For back-off, pass a function as delay; it is given the number of finished runs, so (finished) => timer(finished * wait) waits longer each time. For a fixed beat whatever the answers do, use timer with switchMap instead.

item0.why: Reach for retry when a run should start again after it fails: it is the same loop, subscribing again on an error where repeat does so on completion.

item1.why: Read RepeatConfig when the delay must be a function rather than a number, as back-off needs: it sets out count and delay, notifier form included.

item2.why: repeatWhen is what older code uses to say when to repeat; it is deprecated, and meeting it means rewriting it as repeat with a delay function.

item3.why: Reach for takeWhile after repeat when a poll should stop on an answer rather than after a count.

item4.why: Reach for defer when the source does its work once, at creation, such as a promise: wrapped in defer, each repetition does the work again.

item5.why: Reach for concat when the runs differ, such as one request followed by another; over a cold source, repeat with a count is concat of the source with itself.

item6.why: Reach for timer with switchMap when requests must go out on a fixed beat whatever the answers do; repeat waits for each answer before its next wait.

example.caption: Time runs in frames, left to right. A circle is an emission, with its letter, and a bar is completion. Each grey lane is check$ subscribed again by repeat; the bar that ends each run is held back from status$ until the last run, so status$ has a single bar, at the end. Step the frames to follow each run.

notes.0: The page subscribes to status$, so check$ sends its first request.
notes.1: The first request is out; its answer is not back yet.
notes.2: The first answer, queued, arrives and goes straight through to status$.
notes.3: check$ completes, but status$ does not. repeat counts {{completed}} finished run, sees that the count is not reached and starts the timer for its delay.
notes.4: repeat is waiting out its delay. No request is out.
notes.5: The timer fires. repeat subscribes to check$ again, and the new subscription sends a new request.
notes.7: The second answer, running, goes straight through.
notes.8: The second run completes. Repeat has finished {{completed}} runs, so it waits once more.
notes.9: repeat is waiting out its delay before the last request.
notes.10: The timer fires, and repeat subscribes to check$ for the third and last time.
notes.12: The third answer, passed, goes straight through.
notes.13: The third run completes. That is the count, so repeat completes status$ instead of waiting again.

intuition.text: A plain Subject is a live broadcast: tune in late and what went before is gone. A ReplaySubject keeps a short recording beside the broadcast. A newcomer is played the recording first, all in one go and oldest first, and then joins the live feed, without the source being asked to run again. How much is recorded is set when the subject is made: a number of values, an age, or both.
intuition.situation: A verifier who joins a run partway through needs the latest reports to make sense of what comes next, and the run cannot be repeated for their benefit. A log that keeps the last few reports and plays them to each newcomer gives the verifier a bounded recent history in place of a rerun.

example.name: A run's report log with a late verifier
example.description: An executor posts its reports, {reports}, whether or not anyone is listening, into a log that keeps the newest {bufferSize}. A dashboard subscribes before the first report. A verifier subscribes at frame {verifierJoins}, just after tests ok has been posted, and an auditor at frame {auditorJoins}, after the run has completed.

parameters.reports: lint ok, types ok, tests ok, build ok and docs ok

step0.title: Record each value, keeping the newest few
step0.text: When the source emits, add the value to the end of the buffer. If the buffer now holds more than {bufferSize}, let the oldest go: here lint ok leaves the log when tests ok arrives.

step1.title: Pass it to everyone listening
step1.text: Every current subscriber receives the value at once, exactly as it would from a plain Subject. The buffer exists only for those who come later.

step2.title: Hand a newcomer the buffer, then go live
step2.text: When someone subscribes, add them to the listeners and immediately send them every value still in the buffer, oldest first, inside the subscribe call. The verifier, subscribing at frame {verifierJoins}, receives types ok and tests ok together, then build ok and docs ok as they are posted.

step3.title: Keep replaying after the end
step3.text: When the source completes or errors, end every current subscriber the same way but keep the buffer. Anyone who subscribes afterwards is handed the buffer and then ended at once, which is how the auditor, at frame {auditorJoins}, still sees the last reports of a finished run.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each value from the source:
  add value to the end of buffer
  if buffer holds more values than its size allows:
    let the oldest go

  send value to every current listener

when someone starts listening:
  add them to the current listeners
  send them each value in buffer, oldest first

when the source finishes or fails:
  keep buffer, and remember how the source ended
  tell every current listener the same way
  (a later listener is sent buffer, then told at once)

visual.textEquivalent: The log keeps the newest {bufferSize} reports. Frame {frame}: {now}.

item0.relevance: RxJS itself, the library this app runs on: shareReplay.ts at 7.8.2, the installed version, builds the shareReplay operator on a ReplaySubject.
item0.explanation: shareReplay is share with a ReplaySubject as the connector between a source and its subscribers. Every subscriber subscribes to that one subject, and only the subject subscribes to the source, so an expensive source such as an HTTP request runs once and a later subscriber is replayed its values instead of starting it again. The buffer size and window time pass straight to the ReplaySubject. The subject is kept after the source completes, so a completed result stays cached, but replaced after an error, so a later subscriber retries; with refCount false, the default, the source stays subscribed after the last subscriber leaves.

item1.project: Angular, toObservable in the RxJS interop package
item1.relevance: Angular's bridge from signals to observables, in the angular/angular repository: to_observable.ts at v22.2.3, the installed version.
item1.explanation: An effect reads the signal and pushes each value it sees into a ReplaySubject that keeps one value; the function returns that subject as a plain observable and completes it when its injector is destroyed. Because the subject keeps the latest value, a subscriber that arrives long after the signal last changed is handed the current value at once instead of waiting for the next change: the verifier's catch-up, with a history one value deep.

item0.title: RxJS API reference · ReplaySubject
item0.supports: The buffer size and window time both default to unbounded and a timestamp provider measures age; a new subscriber is sent the buffer synchronously in first-in first-out order; a subject that has completed or errored still replays and then completes or errors the newcomer; unlike a BehaviorSubject it starts empty and keeps replaying after an error.

item1.title: ReplaySubject.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item1.supports: At the installed version next appends the value to the buffer, with an expiry time beside it when the window is finite, and trims the buffer to its size and age; subscribing adds the subscriber, then sends it a copy of the buffer oldest first, then checks whether the subject has already stopped.

item2.title: Subject.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item2.supports: A subscriber that arrives after the subject has stopped is not added to its observers and is errored or completed at once, which is what ends the auditor after its replay.

item3.title: RxJS guide · Subject
item3.supports: The guide's treatment of the subject family: its ReplaySubject examples show an observer that subscribes late receiving only the recent values, bounded first by a count and then by an age in milliseconds, before the live ones; it sets this beside BehaviorSubject's single current value and AsyncSubject's last value on completion.

item4.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item4.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share: a dash is one frame, a letter an emission, a bar completion, parentheses values emitted in the same frame with the group taking as many frames as it has characters, and a caret and an exclamation mark the start and end of a subscription.

limits.item0: Without a bound it remembers everything. new ReplaySubject() with neither a buffer size nor a window time keeps every value for as long as the subject lives, so a long-running log grows without limit and every newcomer is replayed all of it. Give it a size, an age, or both.
limits.item1: Replay arrives in one burst, inside the subscribe call. The verifier is handed {bufferSize} reports at frame {verifierJoins} before its subscribe call returns, so its handler runs for every replayed value before the line after subscribe does. Anything the handler needs must be ready before subscribing.
limits.item2: A replayed value carries no sign that it is old. The verifier cannot tell from types ok alone that it was posted before it joined. Put the time in the value when its age matters, or bound the replay with a window time, which the subject measures with the timestamp provider given to its constructor.
limits.item3: It never forgets an ending. The auditor at frame {auditorJoins} is still handed the last reports and the completion, and a subject that errored goes on replaying its buffer followed by the error. That suits the record of a finished run; to start over, make a new subject, as shareReplay does after an error but not after completion.
limits.item4: Keeping the last value is not holding a current one. A ReplaySubject that keeps one value has nothing to give a subscriber before the first value is posted, and no value to read synchronously. When there is always a current state, a BehaviorSubject says so.

item0.why: bufferSize is the bound this example sets: how many recent values a newcomer is handed.

item1.why: windowTime bounds the replay by age instead of, or as well as, by count, when a report stops mattering after a while rather than after newer ones arrive.

item2.why: A plain Subject has no memory: a newcomer hears only what is posted after it subscribes, so the verifier here would miss every report before build ok.

item3.why: BehaviorSubject is the choice when there is always a current value: it starts with one, hands a newcomer only that one, exposes it synchronously, and stops replaying after an error.

item4.why: AsyncSubject hands a newcomer only the last value, and only once the source has completed: a final result rather than a recent history.

item5.why: shareReplay puts a ReplaySubject between a source and its subscribers, so a cold source runs once and every latecomer is replayed what it produced.

notes.0: The log is empty. The dashboard has subscribed; nobody else has yet.
notes.1: The first report, lint ok, is posted. The log records it and the dashboard hears it.
notes.3: types ok is posted. The log now holds {{held}} reports, as many as it keeps.
notes.5: tests ok is posted. To keep only the newest {{kept}}, the log lets go of lint ok; the dashboard heard it at the time.
notes.6: The verifier subscribes. The log hands it the {{replayed}} reports it holds, types ok and then tests ok, at once and before anything new is posted. lint ok is not among them: the log no longer holds it.
notes.10: build ok is posted. The dashboard and the verifier both hear it live; the log now holds tests ok and build ok.
notes.13: docs ok is posted and both hear it. The log holds build ok and docs ok.
notes.15: The run completes, and so do the dashboard and the verifier. The log keeps its last {{kept}} reports.
notes.18: The auditor subscribes after the run is over. It is handed build ok and docs ok and then completes at once: a finished ReplaySubject still replays.

example.caption: Time runs in frames. A circle is an emission, with its letter; a bar is completion. A subscriber’s lane starts at the frame it subscribes, and circles bunched within one frame arrive together, in order, inside the subscribe call. Step the frames to follow the log.

intuition.text: retry is a bet that the failure was passing. It treats an error as a reason to begin again rather than an ending, and it keeps the bet out of sight: the subscriber sees the values of every attempt but none of the errors until the bet is lost. Whether beginning again means asking the server again depends on the source, not on retry.
intuition.situation: A departures board asking a server over a weak mobile connection. A request that times out often succeeds a moment later, so the board should ask again a couple of times, pausing between tries, before it tells the reader it has failed.

example.name: A departures board that asks up to three times
example.description: The board's request is defer(() => load()), so every subscription calls load() and starts a new attempt. retry allows {count} retries and waits {delay} frames before each. The first attempt times out two frames after it starts, having sent nothing. The second sends the 10:02 a frame after it starts and fails two frames later when its connection is reset. The third sends {departures} and completes.

step0.title: Start an attempt
step0.text: Subscribing calls load(), so the first attempt begins as soon as the board subscribes. Everything retry does later is another subscription to the same deferred request.

step1.title: Pass on what the attempt sends
step1.text: Each value an attempt emits goes to the board at once, whether or not that attempt fails later. retry cannot know yet, and it never takes a value back.

step2.title: On a failure with retries left, wait and ask again
step2.text: retry keeps the error from the board, counts one retry used, waits {delay} frames and subscribes again. The new attempt starts from its beginning.

step3.title: On a failure with none left, give up
step3.text: Once all {count} retries are used, the next error goes to the board and the board fails with it. Only that last error is passed on.

step4.title: Finish with the attempt that finishes
step4.text: When an attempt completes, the board completes. The errors before it were absorbed, and nothing downstream records that they happened.

pseudocode.ordinary:
retries used = 0
start an attempt

on each value from the attempt:
  pass it on
  (even if this attempt fails later)

when the attempt fails and retries used < count:
  retries used = retries used + 1
  wait delay
  start a new attempt
  (the error goes no further)

when the attempt fails and retries used = count:
  fail the output with this error

when the attempt completes:
  complete the output

item0.title: RxJS API reference · retry
item0.supports: retry resubscribes to the source on error, up to count times and without limit when count is omitted, and passes on every value the source emits, including values from subscriptions that later failed.

item1.title: RxJS API reference · RetryConfig
item1.supports: delay is a number of milliseconds or a function returning a notifier whose emission triggers the retry; a notifier that completes without emitting completes the result, one that errors passes its error on, and resetOnSuccess resets the counter when a retried subscription emits.

item2.title: retry.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item2.supports: At the installed version a number delay becomes timer(delay), the counter is reset only when resetOnSuccess is set, and once the count is used up the error goes to the subscriber.

item3.title: Angular guide · Making HTTP requests, Handling request failure
item3.supports: Angular's guide presents retry() as a way to resubscribe a failed HttpClient request a set number of times, for failures such as network interruptions that may clear on their own.

item4.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item4.supports: Inside run, one frame is one virtual millisecond, so retry's delay in milliseconds counts frames in this drawing and its spec.

limits.item0: retry repeats a subscription, not a call. It starts the work over only when subscribing starts it: an HttpClient request does, and so does a source built with defer, as the board's request is. A promise created once and wrapped with from has already failed, so every retry receives the same rejection at once and the server is never asked again.
limits.item1: A failed attempt's values stay delivered: here the 10:02 reaches the board twice. A consumer that counts, appends or acts on each value must tolerate repeats. Upstream it is worse: a write whose answer was lost may already have happened, and retrying it does it again. Retry only what is safe to repeat.
limits.item2: Every error is retried alike. A missing page or a refused request fails the same way each time, and retrying it only delays the failure by {count} waits of {delay} frames. A delay function can tell errors apart: it can return throwError for a permanent error, which then fails at once, and a timer for a transient one. A notifier that completes without emitting stops quietly instead.
limits.item3: The count covers the whole subscription unless resetOnSuccess is set. The 10:02 that the second attempt delivered did not give back the retry it used. On a long-lived feed that fails now and then, the retries run down over its life until one day the error gets through; resetOnSuccess: true restores the count whenever an attempt delivers a value.
limits.item4: Only the last error is passed on; the ones retry absorbed leave no trace, so here the timeout and the reset are invisible to the board. Report each error, in the delay function or with tap before retry, if the evidence matters. Where the reader should decide whether to try again, retry is the wrong tool: show the failure and offer a button, as this app's Tools home does with a Retry button whose press starts a fresh load.

item0.why: catchError replaces a failed source where retry starts it again. Placed after retry, it decides what the reader sees once the retries run out.

item1.why: repeat resubscribes after completion as retry does after an error: polling a request that succeeded is repeat, not retry.

item2.why: defer is what makes each subscription a new attempt, and so what gives retry something to repeat.

item3.why: retryWhen is the older, deprecated form that builds the policy from the stream of errors; code that still uses it moves to retry with a delay function.

item4.why: Retry only what is transient classifies errors before retrying, the delay-function pattern the third limit describes.

item5.why: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter grows the wait with each attempt and spreads clients apart, where this example waits the same delay every time.

example.caption: Time runs in frames, left to right. A circle is an emission, with its letter, and a bar is completion. A cross on an attempt is its error: retry keeps it from board$ and answers with a new attempt, on the next lane, {{delay}} frames later. Step the frames to follow each attempt.

notes.0: The board subscribes, and the first attempt starts.
notes.2: The first attempt fails before sending anything. retry keeps the error from the board, counts {{used}} retry used and starts to wait.
notes.3: retry is waiting out the delay. Nothing reaches the board.
notes.4: The wait is over. retry subscribes again, so load() runs again and a second attempt starts from the beginning. The board has seen no error.
notes.5: The second attempt sends the 10:02, and it goes straight to the board.
notes.7: The second attempt fails part way. Its 10:02 stays on the board. retry counts its second and last retry and waits again.
notes.8: retry waits again. The board still holds the one 10:02 it has received.
notes.9: retry subscribes a third time. If this attempt failed too, its error would reach the board.
notes.10: The third attempt starts from the beginning, so the board receives the 10:02 a second time.
notes.12: The third attempt sends the 10:15, which no earlier attempt reached.
notes.13: The third attempt completes, so the board completes. The {{failures}} errors were absorbed, and the 10:02 arrived {{repeated}} times.

intuition.text: scan lets a stream keep a running answer without anyone keeping a variable. The answer lives inside the subscription and is rebuilt from each event as it arrives, so what is shown is always the history folded so far, and no other code can change it behind the stream's back. It is reduce that reports after every step rather than once at the end, and its state belongs to the subscription that built it, not to the stream.
intuition.situation: A bank statement's balance column: each line is a deposit or a withdrawal, and the balance beside it is the one above plus that amount. The same shape fits any state built from events, such as a basket total, a score or a game's state built from commands. It goes wrong when several readers must share one balance, because each subscription keeps its own.

example.name: A statement and a phone reading one account
example.description: A bank's live feed sends the amounts {amounts} at frames 1, 4 and 8 and completes at frame 11. The balance stream folds them into a balance that opens at {opening}. A statement subscribes to it from the start; a phone app subscribes to the same stream at frame 5, after the first two amounts have gone by.

step0.title: Start each subscriber from the seed
step0.text: When something subscribes, scan gives that subscription its own state, set to the seed: the opening of {opening}. Nothing is sent yet. The phone, subscribing at frame 5, starts from the opening too, not from the balance the statement has reached.

step1.title: Fold each amount into the state
step1.text: When an amount arrives, each subscription's reducer receives that subscription's state and the amount, and its result replaces the state. Without a seed, the first amount would become the state unchanged and the reducer would first run on the second.

step2.title: Send the new state
step2.text: The new state goes out at once, on every amount, so the statement's balance column fills line by line. reduce would keep the same state but send only the last one, when the feed completes.

step3.title: Finish with the feed
step3.text: When the feed completes, each balance stream completes and sends nothing more. An error from the feed, or one the reducer throws, ends the stream with that error, and the state goes with the subscription.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when a reader starts listening:
  give that reader its own balance, set to the opening
  (a reader who starts late still starts from the opening)
  send nothing yet

on each amount from the feed, for each reader:
  if the reader has no balance yet (no opening was given):
    balance = amount
  otherwise:
    balance = balance + amount

  send the reader's new balance

when the feed finishes:
  finish each reader's balances
  (the last balance has already been sent)
if the feed fails, or the addition throws:
  fail the reader's balances with that error

item0.title: RxJS API reference · scan
item0.supports: With a seed every value passes through the accumulator; without one the first value becomes the state and is sent on without passing through it. The state is sent after each update, and an accumulator that throws ends the output with an error.

item1.title: scan.ts in RxJS 7.8.2

item2.title: scanInternals.ts in RxJS 7.8.2

Each value increments the index and replaces the state with the accumulator's result, or with the value itself when there is no state yet. Completion and errors pass straight through.

item4.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item4.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share: a dash is one frame, a letter an emission, a bar completion, a hash an error, and a caret and an exclamation mark the start and end of a subscription.

limits.item0: Each subscription folds on its own, and nothing warns a late one. The phone subscribes at frame 5, starts from the opening and ends on a balance the account never had. When several readers need one running state, fold once and share it: shareReplay(1) after scan gives a late subscriber the current balance at once, and NgRx and this app's scene facade push each state into a BehaviorSubject.
limits.item1: The seed is one value shared by every subscription. A reducer that mutates an object or array seed, rather than returning a new state, changes the seed itself, so the next subscription or a retry starts from the mutated state. Return a new state from the reducer.
limits.item2: Without a seed, the first value becomes the state unchanged and the reducer first runs on the second value, with index 1. That is right only when a value already is a state: leaving out the opening here would take the first deposit for the whole balance. At the installed version a seed of undefined passed explicitly still counts as a seed, because scan counts its arguments.
limits.item3: scan never sends the seed. The statement is blank until the first amount, and the phone shows nothing from subscribing until the next amount arrives. Add startWith(opening) after scan when a fresh fold must show its starting balance at once.
limits.item4: The reducer must be synchronous and should be pure. A reducer that needs a request for each value belongs in mergeScan or switchScan. One with side effects repeats them for every subscription, since each subscription runs its own fold.

item0.why: reduce is the same fold when only the final balance matters: it sends once, when the source completes.

item1.why: mergeScan is the choice when computing the next state needs a stream, such as a request per value; each inner result becomes the next state.

item2.why: switchScan is mergeScan that cancels the computation still in flight when the next value arrives, so only the newest one becomes the state.

item3.why: shareReplay is how several readers share one fold, so a late subscriber receives the current balance instead of starting a new fold from the seed.

item4.why: A BehaviorSubject holds the current state where other code reads it or subscribes late; a folded stream often feeds one, as in NgRx.

item5.why: startWith puts the seed on screen before the first value, which scan itself never does.

notes.0: The statement subscribes. scan holds the opening, {{opening}}, as its state and sends nothing: no amount has arrived yet.
notes.1: A deposit of {{deposit}} arrives. scan adds it to the {{opening}} it holds, keeps the result and sends it: the statement shows {{balance}}.
notes.4: A withdrawal of {{withdrawal}} arrives. The state is now {{before}}, not the opening, so the statement shows {{balance}}.
notes.5: The phone subscribes to the same balance stream. scan starts a separate fold for it from the opening, {{opening}}; the deposit and the withdrawal before this frame are not replayed to it.
notes.8: A deposit of {{deposit}} reaches both folds. The statement adds it to {{before}} and shows {{balance}}; the phone adds it to {{opening}} and shows {{phone}}, a balance the account never had.
notes.11: The feed completes, and both balances complete with nothing more sent: each last balance went out at frame 8.

intuition.text: Where share is a live broadcast, shareReplay is a broadcast with a recording of its last moments: whoever tunes in late hears the recording first and then the live sound, so no reader ever starts empty. The recording is what it costs. To keep it current the source goes on running after the last listener has gone, and a broadcast that has finished is kept and never run again.
intuition.situation: The page of the share study: a stock quote polled from the server, shown in a tile from the start and in a chart the user opens later. Here the chart must draw the current quote the moment it opens rather than sit empty until the next poll, and the question becomes what that convenience costs once the user has left.

example.name: The quote page, with the latest quote kept
example.description: The streams are those of the share study: a poll that fetches a quote every {pollEvery} frames, the first one frame after it starts; the tile subscribing at frame 0; the chart opening at frame {chartOpensAt}; and the user leaving at frame {leftAt}, which unsubscribes both readers. The quote is shared with shareReplay(1), a memory of {bufferSize} quote with refCount left false.

step0.title: Start one run and a memory for the first reader
step0.text: When the tile subscribes, shareReplay creates a memory that holds the latest {bufferSize} quote and subscribes to the poll, once, to fill it. The readers listen to the memory, not to the poll.

step1.title: Store each value, then pass it on
step1.text: Each quote goes into the memory, pushing out the oldest once the memory is full, and on to every reader present at that moment.

step2.title: Replay the memory to a late reader
step2.text: The chart subscribes at frame {chartOpensAt} and is handed the quote in the memory in that same frame, then the live quotes alongside the tile. The memory holds {bufferSize} quote, so that is all the chart is given before the live ones.

step3.title: Keep running when the readers leave
step3.text: At frame {leftAt} both readers unsubscribe. With refCount false, as shareReplay(1) leaves it, having no reader stops nothing: the poll goes on sending requests and filling the memory for no one. With refCount: true it would stop here, and the memory would be dropped with it.

step4.title: Keep a completed run, forget a failed one
step4.text: Had the poll completed, the memory would keep its quote and the completion, and every later reader would receive both at once with no new request. When it fails, the readers present receive the error and end, the memory is dropped, and the next reader starts a new poll with nothing to replay.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the first reader arrives:
  make a memory that holds the latest quote
  start the poll, once, feeding the memory

on each quote from the poll:
  put it in the memory, pushing the older one out
  give it to every reader present at that moment

when a later reader arrives:
  give it the quote in the memory straight away
  then the live quotes, as every other reader gets them

when a reader leaves:
  remove it from the readers present
  (with no reader left the poll keeps running
   and keeps filling the memory, for no one)

when the poll completes:
  keep the memory and the completion: a later reader gets the stored
  quote and the completion at once, and nothing is fetched again
when the poll fails:
  give the failure to every reader present and forget the memory:
  the next reader to arrive is a first reader again
pseudocode.rxjs: shared$ = quote$.pipe(shareReplay(1));

The selector's projection runs once however many template bindings read it; a binding that subscribes later receives the current slice at once, as the chart here receives the stored quote; and because refCount is true, the selector stops listening to the state when its last reader goes instead of outliving it.

item0.title: RxJS API reference · shareReplay
item0.supports: The page states that a completed source is kept for good while a failed one may be subscribed again; that refCount is off by default, so falling to no subscribers leaves the source subscribed, possibly for ever; and that with refCount on the source is let go at that point, and the next subscriber is served by a fresh ReplaySubject and a fresh subscription.

item1.title: shareReplay.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item1.supports: At the installed version shareReplay calls share with a ReplaySubject connector of the given buffer size and window, resetOnError true, resetOnComplete false and resetOnRefCountZero set to refCount, which defaults to false. Without a buffer size the buffer is unbounded, and in the object form refCount is required.

item2.title: share.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item2.supports: The resets shareReplay configures: on an error share discards its subject before passing the error on, so a later subscriber gets a fresh subject and a fresh subscription to the source, with nothing replayed.

item3.title: RxJS guide · Multicasting deprecations
item3.supports: shareReplay is presented as a light layer over the configurable share, and publishReplay followed by refCount is rewritten as share with a ReplaySubject connector and its resets turned off.

item4.title: Angular guide · Making HTTP requests
item4.supports: Subscribing to an HttpClient observable is what sends its request, and every further subscription sends another: the poll here is cold, and without sharing each reader would run its own.

item5.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item5.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share, including a group in parentheses for values given in one frame, and subscription marbles that hold a subscriber back until a later frame, which is how the chart arrives late in this example.

limits.item0: The default never lets go. After frame {leftAt} the poll goes on fetching for no one, and it will do so for as long as the app runs, because shareReplay(1) leaves refCount false. On a stream that belongs to a page or a component, write shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }), which stops the poll with the last reader. Keep the default for a value that should stay warm for the whole application, owned by a long-lived service that can end it.
limits.item1: refCount: true gives up the cache along with the leak. The memory is dropped together with the poll, so a reader who returns after everyone has left starts a new poll and waits for its first quote, exactly as with share. To keep the last quote through a short absence and still stop the poll in the end, use share with a ReplaySubject connector and a delayed resetOnRefCountZero.
limits.item2: A completed source is cached for good. Had the quote been a single request that completed before the chart opened, the chart would receive the stored quote and the completion at once, and the request would never be sent again: there is no invalidation and no expiry. A value that must be refreshed needs a trigger to rebuild from, a refresh stream switched to a new request, with shareReplay after the switch.
limits.item3: Only the newest values are replayed, and they are as old as their fetch. The chart receives the second quote, not the first, and shows it as current although it was fetched before the chart opened. A larger buffer replays more; shareReplay() with no size keeps every value for the life of the stream; and windowTime refuses to replay a value older than the window.
limits.item4: An error is neither kept nor retried. When the poll fails, the readers present receive the error and end, the memory is discarded, and the next reader starts a new poll with nothing to replay. To keep the readers through a failed request, retry before shareReplay, inside the shared part.

item0.why: share is the choice when a late reader can wait for the next value, or when the work must stop with the last reader and start afresh for the next: it keeps no memory and resets on every ending by default.

item1.why: ShareReplayConfig, the object form, is the only way to set refCount: true, and refCount is required there, so writing it out turns the leak trade-off into a visible decision.

item2.why: A ReplaySubject on its own is the choice when the app pushes the values itself rather than sharing a source; as share's connector it gives the same memory with each reset chosen separately.

item3.why: BehaviorSubject is the choice when there is a sensible value before the first fetch, such as a placeholder, so that no reader ever starts empty, or when the app writes the state itself instead of polling it.

item4.why: This analysis is the one to reach for when auditing an app for subscriptions that outlive their views: it names the default refCount as a leak source and the fixes for it.

notes.0: The tile is on the page from the start. shareReplay makes a memory that holds one quote and starts the poll, once, to fill it.
notes.1: The first quote is stored in the memory and shown on the tile.
notes.5: The second quote replaces the first in the memory and goes to the tile.
notes.7: The user opens the chart. shareReplay hands it the quote in the memory, b, in the same frame, so the chart is never empty. The memory holds one quote, so b is all it replays.
notes.9: The third quote reaches both readers and replaces b in the memory.
notes.13: The fourth quote reaches both readers.
notes.15: The user leaves the page and both readers unsubscribe. shareReplay(1) leaves refCount false, so having no reader does not stop the poll.
notes.17: The poll fetches a quote for no one. The request was sent; its answer only replaces the one in the memory.
notes.21: The poll fetches again for no one. With refCount left false, it runs for as long as the app does.

example.caption: Time runs in frames. A circle is an emission, with its letter. quote$ is the poll; tile$ and chart$ are its two readers, and each lane starts where that reader subscribes. A reader's lane ends in a small ring where it left the page; the poll's lane runs on. Step the frames to follow each quote.

intuition.text: One run of the source, for whoever is listening. share stands between a source and its readers: the first reader to arrive starts the source, every later reader joins that same run at the point it has reached, and when the last reader leaves, share stops the source and forgets it, so the next reader starts it over. While anyone listens the stream is hot, and a reader who arrives late has missed what came before; with no one listening it is cold again.
intuition.situation: A page polls a stock quote and shows it twice: in a tile that is there from the start and in a chart the user opens later. Every subscription to an HttpClient call issues a request of its own, so two readers would run two polls. They should share one, and it should stop when the user leaves the page.

example.name: A quote tile and a chart opened later
example.description: The page polls a quote every {pollEvery} frames, the first arriving one frame after the poll starts. The tile subscribes at frame 0; the user opens the chart at frame {chartOpensAt}, between the second and third quotes, and leaves the page at frame {leftAt}, which unsubscribes both readers. The poll never completes on its own. The shareReplay study runs exactly these streams, so the two diagrams differ only in the operator.

step0.title: Start one run for the first reader
step0.text: When the tile subscribes and nothing is running, share subscribes to the poll, once. Every reader that follows listens to this run; none of them starts a poll of its own.

step1.title: Pass each value to the readers present
step1.text: Each quote goes to every reader subscribed at that moment, and share keeps no copy of it.

step2.title: A late reader joins where the run stands
step2.text: The chart subscribes at frame {chartOpensAt}, into the running poll. share has nothing stored to hand it, so the chart stays empty until the next quote arrives for both readers.

step3.title: Stop when the last reader leaves
step3.text: share counts its readers. When the count falls to none, at frame {leftAt} here, it unsubscribes from the poll and forgets it: no further request is sent, and the next reader to arrive starts a new poll as if share had never run.

step4.title: Forget the run when it ends
step4.text: If the poll completes or fails, share passes the completion or the error to the readers present, which ends them, and forgets the run, so the next reader starts a new one. This is a reset, not a retry: the readers who were there have already ended.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when the first reader arrives:
  start the poll, once, for every reader to come

on each quote from the poll:
  give it to every reader present at that moment
  (store nothing: a reader who arrives later never sees it)

when a later reader arrives:
  add it to the readers present
  (it waits for the next quote; nothing is replayed)

when a reader leaves:
  remove it from the readers present
  if none is left:
    stop the poll and forget it
    (the next reader to arrive is a first reader again)

when the poll completes or fails:
  pass that on to every reader present, which ends them
  forget the poll: the next reader to arrive is a first reader again
  (nothing is retried for the readers who were there)
pseudocode.rxjs: shared$ = quote$.pipe(share());

item4.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams
item4.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share, including subscription marbles, where a caret and an exclamation mark give a subscription's start and end and can hold a subscriber back until a later frame, which is how the chart arrives late in this example.

limits.item0: A late reader starts empty. The chart opened at frame {chartOpensAt} has nothing to draw until the next quote, and the quotes fetched before it opened never reach it. Where a reader must show the current value the moment it subscribes, use shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }), or give share a ReplaySubject connector and keep its resets under your own control.
limits.item1: Every reset repeats the work. Once the last reader has gone, or the source has completed or failed, the next reader starts the source again. Had the quote been one request that completed before the chart opened, share would have sent a second request for the chart. That is how two async pipes on one shared HttpClient call can send two requests: the second, rendered only once the first value has arrived, subscribes after the request has completed. A result that should be fetched once belongs behind shareReplay; readers who come and go in quick succession are better served by a delayed reset, resetOnRefCountZero: () => timer(ms), which keeps one poll running through the gap.
limits.item2: A reset is not a retry. If the poll fails, the tile and the chart both receive the error and stop; only a reader that subscribes afterwards starts a new poll. To keep the readers through a failed request, retry inside the shared part, before share, as in quote$.pipe(retry({ count: 3, delay: 1000 }), share()).
limits.item3: A synchronous source is not shared at all. Were the quote served synchronously, from an in-memory cache say, the tile would receive it and the completion inside its own subscribe call, share would reset, and the chart would read the cache a second time. connect, which subscribes every reader before it starts the source, shares such a source once.

item0.why: shareReplay is the choice when a late reader must see the latest value at once, as the chart here would prefer, or when a completed result should be kept rather than fetched again.

item1.why: ShareConfig is where share's defaults change: a delayed resetOnRefCountZero keeps the poll through a quick navigation, and a ReplaySubject connector hands late readers the latest value while share's resets stay on.

item2.why: connect is the choice when every reader is known inside one expression or the source is synchronous: it subscribes them all before it starts the source, so none misses a value and nothing resets in between.

item3.why: connectable is the choice when the shared run must start, and keep running, on your command rather than on the first and last reader, such as a feed warmed up before any view subscribes.

notes.0: The tile is on the page from the start. It is share's first reader, so share starts the poll now, once, for every reader to come.
notes.1: The first quote arrives and the tile shows it. The chart is not open yet.
notes.5: The second quote goes to the tile alone. share keeps no copy of it.
notes.7: The user opens the chart, which subscribes into the poll already running. share has nothing stored to give it, so the chart stays empty.
notes.9: The third quote reaches both readers from the one poll. It is the chart's first quote.
notes.13: The fourth quote reaches both readers.
notes.15: The user leaves the page and both readers unsubscribe. With no reader left, share stops the poll and forgets it; the next reader would start a new one.

A lane that ends in a small ring ends where its subscription did: on a reader, where it left the page; on quote$, where share stopped the poll. Step the frames to follow each quote.

intuition.text: A stream that has not spoken yet leaves its subscriber with nothing to show, and nothing looks the same as broken. startWith lets the code that builds the stream speak first, with a value known before the source has done anything. It is a fixed opening line, not a memory: every subscriber hears the same opening, whenever it arrives, and then whatever the source says from that moment on.
intuition.situation: A status panel subscribes to a worker's reports, but the worker says nothing until it has started. Seeding the stream with an explicit initial status gives the person watching a meaningful state before the first report, instead of an empty panel that could mean waiting, failed or never connected.

example.name: Status panels before and after the worker's first report
example.description: The worker reports {reports}, the first at frame {firstReport}, whether or not a panel is watching, and its status completes at frame {completes}. Panels subscribe to it through startWith with {seed} as the seed: the first as the worker starts, a second at frame {latePanel}, when the worker is already running.

step0.title: Emit the seed on subscription
step0.text: As soon as something subscribes, emit the given values in order, inside the subscribe call. Every subscriber gets them, whenever it arrives: the second panel is shown {seed} at frame {latePanel}, though the worker is running by then.

step1.title: Then subscribe to the source
step1.text: Only once the last seed value has gone out does it subscribe to the source, separately for each subscriber. startWith is concat of its values and the source, so nothing from the source can arrive ahead of the seed.

step2.title: Pass the source through unchanged
step2.text: Each value from the source goes straight to the output. The seed is not held or replaced; it is simply the output's first value, and running takes its place on the first panel when it arrives.

step3.title: End when the source ends
step3.text: The output completes or errors when the source does. The seed has gone out by then, so even a source that fails at once leaves the subscriber having seen it.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when someone starts listening:
  for each seed value, in order:
    send value to the listener

  then start listening to the source on this listener's behalf

on each value from the source:
  send value to the listener

when the source finishes or fails:
  tell the listener the same way
pseudocode.rxjs:
shown$ = status$.pipe(startWith('waiting'));
// Both panels subscribe to shown$: the first at once, the second when it is opened.

visual.textEquivalent: The seed is {seed}. Frame {frame}: {now}.

item0.explanation: The facade turns the router's events into a signal of the current query parameters. NavigationEnd arrives only when a navigation finishes, so on its own the stream would say nothing about the URL the page was reached by. The seed is null and it sits before map, which reads the router's current URL whenever anything arrives: the null is only a trigger, turned into the query as it stands at subscription, and each later NavigationEnd is turned into the query the same way. The facade asks toSignal for requireSync, which throws unless the observable emits during subscribe; startWith's synchronous seed is what satisfies it.

item1.relevance: Angular's router, in the angular/angular repository: prioritized_guard_value.ts at v22.2.3, the installed version, combines the results of a route's guards into one decision.
item1.explanation: Each guard's result stream is cut to its first value and seeded with a private INITIAL_VALUE symbol, so combineLatest has a value from every guard at once and emits again as each guard answers. The map walks the guards in priority order and returns INITIAL_VALUE while an earlier guard is still undecided, so a later guard's refusal cannot win before an earlier guard has answered; a filter then drops the placeholders and the first settled decision is taken. The seed is a value no guard can return, which is how the router tells not yet from an answer.

item2.relevance: The Angular CDK, the component toolkit in the angular/components repository: breakpoints-observer.ts at v22.2.3, the installed version, reports whether media queries match.
item2.explanation: Each media query's change listener is wrapped in an observable, and a change event fires only when the match changes, so on its own the stream would say nothing about whether the query matches now. startWith puts the MediaQueryList itself in front, and the map that follows reads matches from it just as it does from a change event, so a subscriber learns the current state at once. Like the scene facade's null, the seed sits before map and comes out in the same shape as every later value.

limits.item0: The seed is fixed when the pipeline is built, not when someone subscribes. startWith(read()) calls read() once, on the line that builds the pipe, so a pipeline built early and subscribed later starts from a stale value. Seed a trigger and read the value in a map, as the scene facade does with startWith(null), or build the pipeline inside defer.
limits.item1: Every subscription gets the seed again, however late it comes. startWith remembers nothing: the second panel subscribes at frame {latePanel}, after the worker has reported running, and is still shown {seed}; it learns the real status only at the next report. When a newcomer should get the latest status, hold it in a BehaviorSubject or share the seeded stream with shareReplay(1).
limits.item2: The seed is a value like any other. Downstream code cannot tell {seed} from a report the worker sent, so a count of reports, a log of changes or a test of whether the worker has spoken yet will include it. When the difference matters, seed a value the consumer can recognise as no report at all, as the router does with its INITIAL_VALUE symbol.
limits.item3: Where it sits decides what the seed passes through. Placed before map, scan or any other operator, the seed goes through it like a source value; placed after, it comes out exactly as written. The scene facade and the CDK's breakpoint observer both rely on the first: their seed passes through map and comes out shaped like every later value.

item0.why: A BehaviorSubject also gives each subscriber a value at once, but the latest one rather than a fixed seed, so the second panel would see running, not waiting.

item1.why: endWith is the mirror image: values emitted after the source completes instead of before it starts.

item2.why: startWith is concat of its values and the source; concat is the general form when what comes first is itself a stream rather than fixed values.

item3.why: defaultIfEmpty supplies a value only when the source completes without emitting, and at the end rather than the start.

item4.why: combineLatest emits nothing until every input has emitted once; seeding each input with startWith lets it emit from the first subscription, as the router's guard decision does.

item5.why: toSignal with requireSync needs a value during subscription, and a startWith seed is the usual way to guarantee one, as the scene facade does.

notes.9: passed arrives, and both panels show it.
notes.11: The worker’s status completes, and so do both panels’ streams.

intuition.text: Of the subjects, this is the one with no memory. It keeps a list of who is listening and whether it has ended, and nothing else: a value exists only in the instant it is pushed, so whoever is on the list then hears it and whoever arrives later never will. Subscribing costs nothing and starts nothing; the work that produces the values happens once, outside the subject, however many listen.
intuition.situation: The scene's Step button, heard by two parts of the page: the painter, which redraws on every step, and a step log opened partway through. Each press should happen once and reach both, and the log, like a browser's network panel opened after the page has loaded, shows steps from the moment it opens.

example.name: A Step button, a log opened late and a latecomer
example.description: The Step button is pressed three times, {presses}, at frames 2, 6 and 10, and the page closes at frame 14, which ends the presses. Every press goes into one subject. The painter listens from frame 0, the step log subscribes at frame {logOpensAt}, between the first press and the second, and a summary panel subscribes at frame {latecomerArrivesAt}, after the page has closed. In the app a press calls next on the subject; here the presses are an input stream the subject subscribes to, which makes the same calls.

step0.title: Feed the subject once
step0.text: The subject is subscribed to the presses a single time. However many parts of the page listen, each press is produced once and goes into the subject once; a cold stream would instead run its work again for every subscriber.

step1.title: Put each listener on the list
step1.text: Subscribing adds the listener to the subject's list and does nothing else: no work starts for it, and nothing earlier is replayed, because nothing earlier was kept. The log, which subscribes at frame {logOpensAt}, has missed press 1 for good. A listener that arrives after the end is told of the end instead, at once.

step2.title: Hand each value to everyone on the list
step2.text: When a press arrives, the subject hands it to each listener on its list at that moment, one after another within the same frame, so the painter and the log both hear press 2 in the frame it is pressed. The press is not kept once it has been handed round.

step3.title: End everyone together
step3.text: When the presses complete, or fail with an error, the subject passes that ending to every listener, empties its list and stays closed, so a later press would be ignored. The summary panel, subscribing at frame {latecomerArrivesAt}, is told at once that it is over and hears no press.

pseudocode.ordinary:
steps holds a list of listeners and whether it has ended, and no values
connect steps to the presses, once

when a part of the page starts listening to steps:
  if steps has ended: pass on that ending at once, and add nothing
  otherwise: add the listener to the list
  (nothing is replayed: no earlier press was kept)

when a press arrives:
  for each listener on the list at this moment:
    hand it the press
  keep nothing of the press

when the presses end, normally or with an error:
  pass that ending to every listener on the list
  empty the list, and remember that steps has ended
  ignore any press that comes later

visual.textEquivalent: Frame {frame}: {now}.

item0.relevance: Where this app uses it: libs/features/scene/src/lib/clock/scene-clock.ts takes the scene's hand-made steps through a Subject.

item0.title: RxJS API reference · Subject
item0.supports: A Subject is both a stream to subscribe to and a receiver of next, error and complete calls, sharing what it receives among all its subscribers; asObservable keeps that receiving side out of reach of the code it is handed to.

item1.title: Subject.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item1.supports: At the installed version next hands the value to a snapshot of the current observers; complete and error notify and remove every observer; a subscriber arriving after either is told at once; unsubscribe on the subject closes it, so later use throws; and asObservable returns an Observable whose source is the subject.

item2.title: RxJS guide · Subject, at RxJS 7.8.2
item2.supports: Subscribing to a Subject only adds the observer to its listeners and starts no run of its own, so all its observers share one run where a plain Observable gives each subscriber its own; and a Subject can be handed to a source's subscribe to share that source among its observers.

item3.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams, at RxJS 7.8.2
item3.supports: The marble syntax this drawing and its spec share: a dash is one frame, a letter an emission, a bar completion, and a caret the frame a subscription starts.

limits.item0: A Subject remembers nothing. A listener that subscribes late has missed everything before it, as the log misses press 1, and one that subscribes after the end hears only the ending, as the summary panel does. When a late listener needs how things stand rather than what happens next, use a BehaviorSubject; when it needs the last few events, a ReplaySubject with a bounded buffer.
limits.item1: Handing out the subject itself lets any listener call next, error or complete for everyone, so one consumer's complete ends the stream for all the others. Keep it private and expose asObservable, with methods for pushing, as the scene clock does with tick.
limits.item2: A completed or errored subject stays closed: later next calls are dropped without a word, so something that is created again needs a new subject. Calling unsubscribe on the subject itself, rather than on a subscription to it, drops every listener without telling them it is over and makes any later next throw ObjectUnsubscribedError.
limits.item3: Delivery is synchronous and in subscription order. A listener that pushes into the same subject from inside its handler starts a nested round of delivery, so the listeners after it hear the new value before the one it was answering.
limits.item4: A hand-wired subject is state someone must own. Where a creation function already says it, such as fromEvent for a DOM event or from for a promise, prefer it; to share one execution of an existing observable, share makes and manages the subject itself. A subject earns its place where ordinary code pushes values in, as the scene facade's step method does through the clock's tick.

item0.why: Unicast against multicast is the distinction this study rests on: a plain observable runs once for each subscriber, a subject once for all of them.

item1.why: BehaviorSubject is the next memory up: it keeps one value and hands it to each new subscriber, for a state rather than a stream of events.

item2.why: ReplaySubject keeps a bounded number of recent values and replays them to late subscribers, for a listener that needs some of what it missed.

item3.why: AsyncSubject hands over only the last value, and only on completion, for a result computed once.

item4.why: share creates and manages the subject when the aim is to share one execution of an existing observable among its subscribers.

item5.why: Subjects as public API is the rule behind keeping the subject private and exposing asObservable.

notes.0: The subject has been fed the presses, once, and the painter is listening. Nothing has been pressed and the log is not open.
notes.2: Press 1 goes into the subject, which hands it to everyone on its list: only the painter, so far. The subject keeps nothing of it.
notes.4: The log opens and subscribes. It joins the list, and nothing is replayed because nothing was kept: it will never hear press 1.
notes.6: Press 2 reaches the painter and the log in the same frame: one press, handed to each listener in turn.
notes.10: Press 3 reaches both again. Each press was produced once, however many listen.
notes.14: The page closes and the presses end, so the subject completes: it tells both listeners and empties its list.
notes.16: The summary panel subscribes to a subject that has completed. It is told at once that it is over, and hears no press.

A circle is a press it hears, with its letter; a bar is completion. Step the frames to follow each press.

intuition.text: A new request cancels the one still in flight. switchMap opens an inner stream for each value it receives and, the moment the next value arrives, stops listening to the inner stream it had and listens to the new one instead. Only the newest inner stream's values come out.
intuition.situation: A search box that asks for results on each keystroke. What is shown must belong to the latest query, so an answer to an older query that arrives late must never overwrite it.

example.name: A search box with three queries
example.description: The box emits three queries, {queries}, at frames 1, 5 and 7, and completes at frame 14. Each query opens a request whose first page arrives {firstPage} frames later and whose second page {secondPage} frames later, after which the request completes. The second query is cut off before any of its pages arrive.

step0.title: Cut off the request in flight
step0.text: When the box emits a query while a request is still running, stop listening to that request first. Whatever it returns later falls on the floor; that is the switch, and it is why no stale page can appear.

step1.title: Open a request for the new query
step1.text: Then start the request for the query that just arrived and keep it as the one in flight.

step2.title: Pass on what the request in flight delivers
step2.text: Each page the request in flight returns goes straight to the output.

step3.title: Finish only when both are done
step3.text: The output completes once the box has completed and the request in flight has delivered everything it will; a box that completes while a request is running leaves the output open until that request completes.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each query from the box:
  if a request is still running:
    stop listening to it
    (anything it returns later is ignored)

  request = start fetching the pages for query

on each page from the current request:
  show page

when the box has completed and the current request has completed:
  complete the output

visual.textEquivalent: Frame {frame}: {now}. Shown so far: {delivered}.

item0.supports: switchMap projects each source value to an inner observable and passes on only the latest inner's values, stopping the earlier inner's the moment a new source value arrives.

item1.title: switchMap.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
