item2.supports: In DotLn the operator's resume phrase is the dispatch that starts a role's work; when the router drives an order it starts each phase in a new worker session given only that phase's phrase; a dispatch is refused while another session holds the work; and each role dispatch is bounded by limits on elapsed time and complete runs, past which further gates and launches are refused until the operator accepts an overrun.

item3.title: DotLn domain model (docs/product/02-domain-model.md) at commit 9139d91 · Beacon perception and age
item3.supports: A beacon reading calls a beacon stale once its age at the reading reaches the set threshold, twenty minutes unless changed, labels a beacon whose modification time is later than the reading as clock skew, and the age it reads never changes what anyone is permitted to do.

item4.title: concatMap.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item4.supports: At the installed version concatMap is mergeMap with a concurrency of one.

item5.title: mergeInternals.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item5.supports: When the concurrency limit is reached, a source value is pushed onto a buffer, and the projection is called for it only when an inner subscription completes and the value is taken off the buffer; so in this example the age is read at the moment of taking.

limits.item0: Expiration decides which waiting request is lost; it does not shorten the wait. Raise the limit until b is still within it at step 8, and b holds the verifier for its whole verification while c, which arrived young, waits behind it and can expire in its place. When requests expire because one consumer cannot keep up, more consumers on the same channel help; tuning the limit only moves the loss.
limits.item1: The limit is checked only when the verifier is free, so an expired request sits in the queue until its turn comes and the dead letter channel learns of it late. Brokers that also sweep their queues, as Apache Artemis does every thirty seconds by default, narrow that gap; neither removes a message at the instant it expires.
limits.item2: An expiry time compares two clocks: the one that set it and the one that reads it. Skew makes a fresh message look stale or a stale one fresh, which is why Camel's page asks for clocks kept in step and why DotLn labels a beacon whose time lies after the reading as clock skew rather than fresh or stale. Setting and checking on one clock, the channel's own, as this example does, avoids skew, at the price of not counting the time a message took to reach the channel.
limits.item3: The limit governs waiting, not working: once the verifier has a request nothing checks the limit again, and a long verification overruns freely. Bounding the work needs a timeout on the work itself. Here the analogy breaks: DotLn bounds how long a running piece of work may take and refuses to start more until the operator accepts the overrun, and it refuses a second dispatch outright while another session holds the work, instead of queueing it, so a request there is refused rather than left waiting to expire.
limits.item4: A dead letter channel is only a record if someone reads it. Unread, it turns expiry into silent loss and grows without bound; Artemis, for one, can let expired messages expire in their turn, which trades the record for the space.

item0.why: Dead Letter Channel is where expired messages go here; read it when deciding who watches that channel and what happens to a message once it lands there.

item1.why: The expiration mechanics are the next question once the limit matters: an absolute expiry time or a time-to-live, skewed clocks, and replies that expire.

item2.why: Competing Consumers is the choice when messages expire because one consumer cannot keep up: several consumers on the channel shorten the wait instead of moving the loss.

item3.why: Request-Reply is where the late message is a reply: a requester that has stopped waiting needs its reply to expire too, or it acts on an answer nobody still wants.

item4.why: Guaranteed Delivery is the opposite pressure, keeping every message until it is acknowledged; reach for it when losing a message is worse than acting on it late, and pair the two when a kept message can outlive its use.

example.operator: concatMap: past {{timeToLive}} steps to deadLetter$, else to the verifier

notes.0: The operator has {{orders}} orders to be verified and has sent nothing yet. The Request queue is empty and the Verifier is free.
notes.1: The operator sends a, a request to verify order 31, to the Request queue, with a time limit of {{timeToLive}} steps.
notes.2: The Verifier is free, so the Request queue hands a to it, and the Verifier starts verifying order 31.
notes.3: The operator sends b, a request to verify order 32, to the Request queue, with the same limit of {{timeToLive}} steps. The Verifier is busy, so b waits.
notes.4: Nothing moves. b waits in the Request queue while the Verifier works on order 31.
notes.5: The operator sends c, a request to verify order 33, to the Request queue, where it waits behind b.
notes.6: Nothing moves. b and c both wait while the Verifier works on order 31.
notes.7: Nothing moves. b has now waited its whole limit of {{timeToLive}} steps, and the Verifier is still busy with order 31.
notes.8: The Verifier finishes order 31 and is free. The oldest request waiting, b, is now past its limit, so the Request queue moves it to the Dead letter channel instead of handing it to the Verifier.
notes.9: The Request queue hands c, still within its limit, to the Verifier, which starts verifying order 33.
notes.10: The Verifier finishes order 33. Orders 31 and 33 were verified; order 32 never was, and the Dead letter channel keeps its request where someone can see it.

example.caption: Time runs in frames, one step of the flow each. request$ is what the operator sends: a, b and c are requests to verify orders 31, 32 and 33. A verification lane runs from the frame the Verifier receives a request to the bar where it finishes; it carries no values and only keeps the Verifier busy, and there is none for b. toVerifier$ shows each request as it reaches the Verifier, one frame after the queue lets it go, and deadLetter$ each request that was past its limit when its turn came.

flow.caption: Each token is one request from the operator, the person directing the work, to verify an order: a, b and c ask for orders 31, 32 and 33. The Operator box sends them. The Request queue is the channel they wait in, each carrying the step until which it is still worth starting. The Verifier works on one request at a time, and the Dead letter box is a second channel that keeps the requests that waited too long, unverified, where someone can see them. The words in a box say what that box is doing or holding. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

intuition.text: Keep a diary of the traffic without stopping it. Each time a record is handed on, a note about it is dropped into a box beside the road, and the hand-over carries on without waiting. Long after the records themselves have been used up and gone, questions about what happened are put to the box, never to the people doing the work. What the box can answer depends on what each note kept, and on every note arriving.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model and its audit document: an order's records pass from the executor to the verifier and on to the reviewer, and each order also owns an append-only control segment in the control log, from which indexes and other views are rebuilt. Read that log, with its indexes, as this pattern's store: the hand-overs are the live flow and the log is the record of it. For each kind of record one then decides whether its entry keeps the whole record or only its envelope, much as the audit document's fidelity levels run from a short receipt up to complete event envelopes. Audit, in turn, reads the log and never the hand-overs in progress, as the document's audit projections are folds over the retained log.

example.name: The audit reads the control log after the work is done
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public domain model and audit document: the executor hands the evidence of orders 31 and 32 to the verifier, and the verifier files a report on each with the reviewer. Every hand-over also fires a copy at the control log, which keeps {keptInFull} in full and only the envelope of {envelopeOnly}. The audit questions the log about order 31 once the reviewer has finished with it, and later about order 32. The log is down for one hand-over.

step0.title: Fire a copy beside the work
step0.text: When a role sends a record on the work channel, it also sends a copy to the store on a channel of its own, and waits for no answer. The hand-over never depends on the copy arriving.

step1.title: Decide what each kind of copy keeps
step1.text: For each kind of record the copy keeps either the whole record or only its envelope: which record, on which channel, when. Here the log keeps {keptInFull} in full, because their verdicts answer later questions, and only the envelope of {envelopeOnly}, whose content stays with the roles.

step2.title: Keep what arrives
step2.text: The store appends each copy it receives and sends nothing back into the flow. A copy that arrives while the store is down is lost, and nobody in the flow is told.

step3.title: Answer from the store alone
step3.text: Questions about the flow go to the store, which can answer them after the records themselves have been consumed. An answer is only as complete as the copies that arrived: a lost copy looks the same as a record that was never sent.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when a role sends a record to the next role on the work channel:
  send the record on the work channel
  send copyOf(record) to the store on the copy channel, without waiting

copyOf(record):
  if record is a verification report: keep it whole
  otherwise: keep only its envelope (which record, which channel, which step)

when the store receives a copy:
  if the store is up: append the copy to its entries
  otherwise: the copy is lost, and no one is told

when the audit asks about an order:
  look up that order's entries in the store
  answer from those entries alone
  (a record whose copy was lost is simply missing)

visual.textEquivalent: At step {step}, {moves}. Work records travel between the roles, copies travel to the control log on a channel of their own, and the audit asks only the log. Now {states}; {held}.

item0.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging and integration framework. Its reference has a Message Store page in its System Management part, and the name means something different there that a reader of Spring code will meet first.
item0.explanation: Spring Integration reads the pattern as durable buffering. Components that hold messages for a while, such as a QueueChannel or an aggregator, take a message-store attribute, so what they hold can survive a failure; behind one MessageStore interface sit an in-memory default and JDBC, Redis, MongoDB and Hazelcast stores. That is a store of messages still in flight rather than an archive of copies for reporting. The page is plain about what persistence costs: payloads and headers are serialised, the JDBC store by default drops headers that cannot be serialised, and a temporary reply channel carried in a header does not survive the trip through a persistent queue.

item1.relevance: NServiceBus is a .NET messaging framework from Particular Software. Its auditing feature is close to the pattern as the catalog draws it: copies of the traffic gathered in one place for later diagnosis.
item1.explanation: An endpoint set up to audit forwards a copy of every message it has processed successfully to a central audit queue, with added headers giving the processing start and end times, the host and the endpoint; a message that fails goes to the error queue instead and is not copied. ServiceControl reads the audit queue to serve the platform's diagnostic and visual tools. The page is frank about the costs: turning auditing on for every endpoint sends twice as many messages through the system, some message types can be left out with a custom pipeline behaviour, and an audit queue nobody drains can fill until no endpoint that audits into it can process messages.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Message Store
item0.supports: The pattern's page sets the problem of reporting on what messages carried without disturbing a messaging system whose parts are loosely joined and whose messages do not last, and answers it with one central store: each message is duplicated onto a separate channel, by the component that sends it or by a wire tap, and the page treats that channel as part of the Control Bus. Sending the duplicate without waiting keeps the main flow at its pace but adds network traffic, which is why the page suggests keeping only a few key fields, such as the message's id, its channel and a timestamp.

item1.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe and Woolf, Addison-Wesley, 2003), chapter 11, System Management, section Message Store
item1.supports: The book covers the Message Store pattern in chapter 11, System Management; the publisher's page lists the book and that chapter in its table of contents.

item2.title: DotLn domain model · Actors and episodes
item2.supports: In the platform every order has its own append-only control segment; one shared fold works out lifecycle legality and evidence separately for each order, and selection picks the order to look at; and each completion records who performed it, with the harness, model and effort used.

item3.title: DotLn · Audit, records, resilience, and privacy
item3.supports: The platform's audit document, in its Fidelity levels section, ranges from an M0 beacon and an L0 receipt up to L4 governed raw, which keeps the complete event envelopes, and warns that more fidelity is not better in itself, because every level serves its own readers under its own access and retention rules. Its Audit projections section builds the audit views by folding one kept JSONL log without reading or writing anything else, so they can be rebuilt at will, and its Persistence and recovery classes section treats the event log as the authoritative record and Markdown, dashboards and indexes as derived views that can be thrown away and rebuilt from it.

limits.item0: A copy fired and forgotten can be lost, and the flow never notices. When the log is down, the evidence of order 32 still reaches the verifier but its copy does not, so the audit later finds a passing report with nothing behind it, and from the log alone it cannot tell a lost copy from evidence that was never handed over. Where the store must be complete, send the copies with guaranteed delivery and pay for it in storage and acknowledgements, or reconcile the store against counts the flow keeps for itself.
limits.item1: Keeping only the envelope saves traffic and keeps sensitive content out of a second place, but some questions then have no answer: here the log can say that evidence 31 was handed over and never what it contained. Keeping every record whole doubles what is stored and copies whatever the records hold into a store with its own access and retention duties. DotLn's audit document makes the same point: more detail is not better in itself, since each level of detail serves its own readers under its own access and retention rules. When content is needed later but should not travel twice, a claim check keeps it once and passes a key.
limits.item2: The copies are not free. Each record sent becomes two messages, and if the store stops reading, its channel fills: NServiceBus's documentation warns that an audit queue nobody drains can grow until no endpoint auditing into it can process messages, so a stalled store can halt the very flow it was meant to leave alone. Size the copy channel, and watch the store's own backlog on the control bus.
limits.item3: The store sees only what crosses channels. It records that the executor handed evidence 31 to the verifier, not what the verifier did with it or whether it dropped it inside; a component's own decisions need its own reports, or a smart proxy or a pair of taps around it.
limits.item4: Here the analogy breaks: DotLn's control log is not a side copy. Each order's control segment is append-only, the shared fold derives the order's lifecycle legality from it, and indexes and Markdown views are projections rebuilt from that canonical log. Losing a message store leaves the flow running with a blind spot; losing DotLn's log would lose the order's recorded state. The platform's log is closer to an event-sourced record than to this pattern's archive, and a gap like this example's would be a defect there rather than an accepted cost.

item0.why: Reach for a wire tap when a channel's senders cannot be changed to send copies themselves: the tap copies every message on the channel to the store's channel and leaves the flow as it was.

item1.why: Use a message history when a message should carry its own path, for debugging it while it travels, with no central store and no extra channel.

item2.why: Read this comparison when choosing between history carried in the message, gone once the message is consumed, and a central store, which keeps everything but needs copies and storage.

item3.why: Use a claim check when the content itself must be kept for later but should not travel with every message or be stored twice: it is kept once and a key travels instead.

item4.why: The copy channel is management traffic: read the control bus for the separate channels it rides on, and for keeping watch on the store itself.

item5.why: Reach for guaranteed delivery on the copy channel when a lost copy is not acceptable, at the price of storing and acknowledging every copy at each hop.

example.caption: Each token is one message. e and r are the evidence and the verifier's report on order 31, and E and R the same records on order 32; they travel between the roles on the work channel. 1, 2, 3 and 4 are the copies of e, r, E and R, fired at the Control log on a channel of their own: 1 and 3 keep only an envelope saying which record went where and when, 2 and 4 the whole report. q and Q are the Audit's questions about orders 31 and 32, and a and A the log's answers. The Executor, the Verifier and the Reviewer are the roles doing the work; the Control log is the message store, keeping every copy that reaches it; the Audit is whoever questions the flow afterwards, and it asks only the log. The words in a box say what that box is doing, and the tokens in a box are the messages it holds. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

start.note: Nothing has moved. The audit will learn about the work only from what reaches the control log.

0.note: The executor sends e, evidence 31, to the verifier and at the same moment fires 1, its envelope, at the control log: which record, on which channel, at which step. The hand-over does not wait for the log.

1.note: The verifier sends r, its report on order 31, to the reviewer and fires 2, a copy of the whole report, at the log. A report is short and its verdict matters later, so its copy keeps it all.

2.note: The reviewer finishes with r and lets it go. No role holds anything of order 31 any more; only the log's entries remain.

3.note: The audit sends q, a question about order 31, to the log. It asks the log, not the roles or the work channel.

4.note: The log sends back a: evidence 31 was handed over and report 31 passed. It cannot say what the evidence contained, because 1 kept only its envelope.

5.note: The log is down when the executor sends E, evidence 32, to the verifier. E arrives, but 3, its envelope, is lost, and nothing in the work notices.

6.note: The log is up again when the verifier sends R, its report on order 32, to the reviewer, so 4, the copy of R, is kept.

7.note: The audit sends Q, a question about order 32, to the log.

8.note: The log sends back A: report 32 passed, with no evidence behind it. E was handed over, so the gap is in the record and not in the work, but from the log alone the audit cannot tell a lost copy from evidence never sent.

intuition.text: A translator lets two parties keep their own formats. It stands on the channel between them, reads each message in the shape the sender writes, writes the same message in the shape the receiver reads, and then forgets it: it keeps no state, so one message in is one message out, at once and in order. The plumbing is the easy part, a single map in RxJS. The work is in the mapping: deciding what each field becomes, and what to write where the old shape has nothing to say.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against this app's catalog loader at its pinned commit. The catalog loads each book's rows as one bundle, a chunk, and accepts a chunk in the older tool-v0 shape or in tool-v1. Each tool-v0 row goes through a temporary compatibility reader that adds what tool-v1 expects: a definition saying the old catalog has none, and a verification marked partial because no reading of the source is available. Read as messaging, a legacy chunk is a sender that writes only tool-v0, the Tools home, the catalog's front page, is a receiver that reads only tool-v1, and the compatibility reader is the translator between them: neither end changes, and only the reader knows both shapes. DotLn's own documents describe the same move, read here as analogies too: a status page generated from an order's history, and one reviewed source rendered for different readers with its facts unchanged.

example.name: Three legacy rows read for the Tools home
example.description: As an analogy, read against this app's catalog loader: suppose a book's chunk were still in {from}. It holds three rows, {rows}, and sends one at each of frames 1, 2 and 3 before finishing at frame 4. The Tools home reads only {to}. The translator rebuilds each row in {to} in the frame it arrives: it keeps the id, marks the definition unavailable and the verification partial, and keeps nothing between rows.

parameters.rows: eip:60 Message Translator, eip:145 Normalizer and eip:146 Canonical Data Model

step0.title: Take one row as it was written
step0.text: The translator receives a row from the {from} channel. It knows the sender's shape and nothing else about the sender, and the sender knows nothing about the Tools home.

step1.title: Refuse a shape it does not know
step1.text: If the row is not in {from}, there is no mapping to apply, and a guess would hand the Tools home a row that looks right and is not. The translator stops with an error naming the shape. In this reading the error ends the stream; the limits say what to do when the other rows should still flow.

step2.title: Rebuild the row in the receiver's shape
step2.text: Keep what both shapes share, the row's id, and write the fields {to} adds. Where {from} has nothing to say, say so plainly: the definition is marked unavailable and the verification partial, never filled with something plausible.

step3.title: Send it on at once, keeping nothing
step3.text: The new row leaves on the {to} channel in the frame the old one arrived. Nothing is kept for the next row, so the translator never reorders, merges or holds rows back: one row in is one row out.

step4.title: Complete with the sender
step4.text: When the chunk completes, the translator completes the {to} channel. It has nothing left to flush, because it never held anything.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each row from the tool-v0 channel:
  read its id and the shape it says it is in

  if the shape is not tool-v0:
    stop with an error naming the shape
    (no row after this one is translated)

  new row = the same id,
            shape tool-v1,
            definition marked unavailable,
            verification marked partial

  send new row on the tool-v1 channel now
  (nothing is remembered for the next row)

when the chunk completes:
  complete the tool-v1 channel

visual.textEquivalent: Frame {frame}: {moves}. The legacy chunk writes to the {from} channel and the Tools home reads the {to} channel; {states}. The Tools home has received: {delivered}.

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are assembled from the Enterprise Integration Patterns, and its documentation gives this pattern a page of its own.
item0.explanation: Camel offers several ways to translate a message on a route: a transform or set-body step with an expression, a processor or bean that converts the body in Java, and a templating component, Velocity in the page's example, that renders the new body from a template; data formats that marshal and unmarshal between encodings are a further way, which the page leaves to the Marshal page. Each worked example, shown in Java, XML and YAML, is a route that takes a message from one endpoint, converts it and passes it on, so the translator is one step on the route and the endpoints at either end never see each other's format.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's messaging framework. It implements this pattern as its transformer endpoint, documented on its own page, though the page does not use the pattern's name.
item1.explanation: A transformer sits between an input and an output channel and converts the payload, or the whole message, so a producer need not know what type the next consumer expects. It can be a plain method marked @Transformer, a transform step in the Java DSL or an XML element, and the framework ships ready-made ones for strings, maps, JSON, Java serialisation, Avro and Protocol Buffers. Two details stand out: a transformer may not return null, which raises a MessageTransformationException, and the page points a step whose result is optional to a service activator instead; and the page states that Spring Integration does not require a canonical data model or any particular format, leaving that choice to the application.

item2.relevance: Kafka Connect moves records between Apache Kafka and other systems through connectors, and its single message transformations are translators declared in a connector's configuration rather than written as code.
item2.explanation: The Kafka 4.1 user guide describes transformations as lightweight changes made one message at a time, listed as aliases in the order they apply. Its worked example wraps each line read from a file in a map with HoistField and then adds a static field naming the source with InsertField, so plain strings become structured records; other built-in transformations filter or rename fields, cast types, mask fields and convert timestamps, and predicates limit a transformation to the records that match.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Message Translator
item0.supports: The pattern's page in the authors' public catalogue, in its Messaging Systems section: it sets out the problem of applications with their own data formats exchanging messages, places a translating filter between them, and compares it with the Adapter of object-oriented design.

item1.title: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 3: Messaging Systems, Message Translator
item1.supports: The book covers the Message Translator in Chapter 3, Messaging Systems.

item2.title: DotLn-Angular · libs/shared/catalog/src/lib/catalog-loader.ts
item2.supports: The loader accepts a work's chunk in tool-v0 or tool-v1. It returns tool-v1 rows as they are and maps each tool-v0 row through upgradeLegacyTool, a temporary compatibility reader that adds a definition saying the legacy catalog has none, an empty place, related and hooks, and a partial verification note; a chunk in any other shape throws, and the failed load is forgotten so a retry can run.

item3.title: DotLn · Architecture, Session lifecycle and resilience
item3.supports: Resume control keeps an append-only JSONL history for each order and generates a human projection, docs/control/current.md, from those histories; the histories are canonical and the Markdown is disposable.

item4.title: DotLn · Publication compiler
item4.supports: The publication compiler builds editions for different audiences from the same reviewed sources; audience selection may change sequence, vocabulary, examples and depth but not facts, limitations, permissions or evidence, and implementation status labels must stay visibly different in every edition.

limits.item0: A translator can only write what it can derive. Where {from} has nothing to say, an honest translator marks the gap, as this one marks the definition unavailable; one that fills it with a plausible default turns missing data into wrong data that looks right. If the receiver really needs the value, a Content Enricher that looks it up is the tool, not a cleverer mapping.
limits.item1: A record it cannot read is the hard case. In this reading the translator throws, and an error ends an RxJS stream, so rows$ stops at that record and every later row is lost, readable or not: had a row in tool-v2 arrived in place of n, the Tools home would have received only T, and c would never have been read. When the other rows should still flow, catch the failure for each record and send the bad one to an Invalid Message Channel; stopping, as the catalog loader does for a chunk of an unsupported shape, is right only when a partial answer would mislead.
limits.item2: The meaning has to survive the mapping. A translator that maps two different source values to the same target value loses the difference for good, and no later step can recover it. DotLn's publication rules guard against exactly this for implementation status labels, which must stay distinct in every edition however much else is adapted.
limits.item3: Translators between pairs multiply. Two formats need one translator each way; when several parties each keep a format of their own, the pairs grow with roughly the square of their number, and a canonical data model, with one translator in and one out for each party, becomes the cheaper thing to maintain.
limits.item4: Where the analogy breaks: the catalog loader upgrades a whole chunk at once inside one promise and reads the shape from the chunk rather than from each row, so the Tools home receives every row together when the chunk resolves. The rows' separate frames, and each row naming its own shape, are the messaging reading, not the loader's schedule.

item0.why: Reach for a Canonical Data Model when more than two parties each keep their own format: each then needs one translator in and one out, not one for every partner.

item1.why: A Content Enricher is the choice when the receiver needs data the sender never had: it looks the value up or computes it, where a translator can only mark the gap.

item2.why: A Normalizer is the choice when one kind of message arrives in several formats: it routes each to the translator for its format so that all of them come out in one.

item3.why: An Invalid Message Channel is where a message the translator cannot read should go when the other messages must keep flowing, instead of ending the stream.

item4.why: A Content Filter is the choice when the receiver needs less than the sender writes: it removes or flattens fields rather than rewriting the shape.

item5.why: A Channel Adapter is the choice when the other party is not on the messaging system at all; it connects the application, and translating its data remains a separate step.

notes.0: Nothing has moved yet. The legacy chunk holds {{inputCount}} rows: t, n and c.
notes.1: The chunk sends t, the Message Translator row, to the translator, which hands T, the same row rebuilt in tool-v1, to the Tools home in the same step.
notes.2: The chunk sends n, the Normalizer row, to the translator, which hands N to the Tools home. Nothing of t was kept, so n is rebuilt exactly as t was.
notes.3: The chunk sends c, the Canonical Data Model row, to the translator, which hands C to the Tools home: {{outputCount}} rows out for {{inputCount}} in, in the order they were sent.
notes.4: The chunk has no more rows and finishes, so the translator finishes the tool-v1 channel too, with nothing left over to send.

flow.caption: Legacy chunk is a bundle of catalog rows still written in the old shape, tool-v0; Translator is the pattern’s part, which rebuilds each row; Tools home is the catalog page, which reads only the new shape, tool-v1. A token is one row: t, n and c are the Message Translator, Normalizer and Canonical Data Model rows as the chunk wrote them, and T, N and C the same rows rebuilt in tool-v1. A row and its rebuilt copy move in the same step, because the translator hands each row on as soon as it arrives. A token is green while it moves and outlined while a box holds it; a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green, and the words inside a box say what it does. Step forward to move the rows on.

intuition.text: A process manager is the one place that knows how far each run of a process has got. The steps never address each other: each answers the manager, and the manager reads that answer against everything it has recorded for the run before it picks the next step. Keeping that record in one place is what lets a route branch on a result, go round a loop and stop at a limit; it is also why every message has to pass through the manager.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide, in its section on the operator's resume phrases. An order passes from an executor, which builds it, to a verifier, which checks it, and on to a reviewer for a final review; a failed verification sends it back to the executor for repair before it is checked again. Each worker is started by a phrase, a short command such as resume: verify. When the operator types each phrase by hand, the operator is the manager, looking at the order's status and choosing what comes next. drive: WO-NNN hands that role to a router: it consults nothing but the order's status, starts a fresh worker for the single phrase that status calls for, and looks at status once more after that worker finishes. The order's progress is already kept in a record, its append-only log, rather than in anyone's head, so whoever reads that record can take the manager's place.

example.name: Driving one order through a repair loop
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. The operator drives {order} at frame 1. Each worker reports to the router one frame after the phrase that started it, and the router sends its next phrase one frame after reading a report, so one message moves at each step: the executor builds the order, the first verification fails, the executor repairs it, the second verification passes and the final review passes. The router counts failed verifications against a limit of {failureLimit} and, after the final review, stops and asks the operator to merge. The reports are scripted at the frames a worker would finish; the router only ever sees them arrive.

step0.title: Start an instance on the trigger
step0.text: The drive names an order. A record of that order starts, with no step done and no failures, and the router sends the first phrase, resume: next, to the executor.

step1.title: Fold each report into the record
step1.text: Every report that reaches the router is folded into the order's record: which step has just finished and how many verifications have failed so far.

step2.title: Decide the next phrase from the record
step2.text: The record, not the report alone, picks the next step. The executor's reports that the order is built (implementation-ready) or repaired (repair-complete) both send it to the verifier; a passed verification sends it on to final review; a failed one sends it back to the executor for repair while fewer than {failureLimit} verifications have failed.

step3.title: Stop the route
step3.text: A passed final review ends the route, and so does a failed verification that reaches the limit of {failureLimit}. The router sends its stop to the operator and reads no more reports for this order.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on drive for an order:
  record = { order, failures: 0 }
  send resume: next to the executor

on each report for that order:
  update the record with the report
  if the report is a failed verification:
    record.failures = record.failures + 1

decide the next phrase from the record:
  implementation-ready or repair-complete: send resume: verify to the verifier
  failed verification, failures below the limit: send resume: fix to the executor
  passed verification: send resume: final review to the reviewer

if the final review passed, or failures reached the limit:
  send the stop to the operator
  read no more reports for this order

visual.textEquivalent: Step {step} of driving {order}: {moves}. {states}. Every report comes to the Router and every phrase leaves it, each phrase decided from the Router's record of the order. Phrases sent so far: {delivered}.

item0.relevance: Apache Camel, the open-source Java integration framework, has a page for the pattern, and it answers by pointing to another of its patterns.
item0.explanation: Camel's page for the pattern says it builds a process manager from its Dynamic Router, which keeps track of how far the message has got and works out each next step as it goes. The Dynamic Router's own page, cited among the references, gives the mechanics: unlike a routing slip, which is worked out once at the start, the router's expression is evaluated again after every step until it returns null; one that never returns null keeps routing for ever; and state kept between evaluations belongs in the exchange's properties, so that concurrent messages do not share it. In Camel the record therefore travels with the exchange rather than sitting in a store of its own.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration, which brings these patterns to Spring applications, gives the pattern a page among its routers.
item1.explanation: It builds a process manager on its routing slip: the custom logic sits in a RoutingSlipRouteStrategy, which receives the request message and the previous step's reply and returns where the message goes next. Because the strategy may return any MessageChannel, including one created on the spot rather than declared as a bean, the next step can be chosen when nothing could have predicted it; the page's example returns a channel whose handler differs with the type of the payload.

item2.relevance: NServiceBus, Particular Software's service bus for .NET, calls its process managers sagas, and its page sets out what holding a long-running process's state involves.
item2.explanation: A saga is a message-driven state machine: a class with separately declared data that is persisted between messages. Named message types start an instance when no existing one matches, and every handled message is mapped to its instance through a correlation property such as the order's id. The page warns that messages can arrive out of order and that a saga not designed for that will discard some of them, and a handler marks the saga complete when the process is over.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Process Manager
item0.supports: The pattern's catalog entry, filed under Message Routing, describes the hub-and-spoke flow from a trigger message through each processing unit's reply back to the central unit, warns that the central unit can become a performance bottleneck and that using one for every problem is overkill, and names AWS Step Functions and GCP Workflows as the process managers of its serverless loan broker examples.

item1.title: Hohpe and Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 7: Message Routing, Process Manager
item1.supports: The book covers Process Manager in its chapter 7, Message Routing; the publisher's page lists that chapter in the book's contents.

item2.title: DotLn execution guide, pinned · Operator resume phrases — how you get dispatched
item2.supports: DotLn's execution guide describes drive: WO-NNN as handing an order to a router that consults only canonical status, starts a fresh worker for the phrase status calls for and rereads status afterwards, holding no writer; it lists, among the ends of a drive, the operator's merge, a third failed verification and a second failed final review; it has resume: fix repair the order and repair-complete recorded before the order is verified again; it computes status by folding the order's append-only event records; and it turns away a transition the lifecycle does not allow without writing anything.

item3.title: Apache Camel · Dynamic Router
item3.supports: Camel's Dynamic Router works out the next endpoint again after every step until its expression yields null, warns that an expression that never yields null makes it repeat without end, contrasts this with a routing slip computed once at the start, and advises keeping state between calls on the exchange for thread safety.

limits.item0: Every step depends on the manager. If its record of an order lived only in memory, a crash would forget how far every order had got; here the record is a fold of the order's log, so a fresh router can read it again, and a process manager without such a store needs one before it can be trusted with long processes. Every message also passes through it, so it is where load gathers.
limits.item1: A loop needs a bound counted in the record. Without the limit of {failureLimit} failed verifications, a verifier that never passes would keep the order cycling between fix and verify for ever; once {failureLimit} have failed, the next phrase is a stop, not another fix.
limits.item2: The manager has to match each report to its instance and to the step it is waiting for. Read without that check, a late or repeated report would set off a second dispatch. DotLn's lifecycle turns away a transition it does not allow without recording anything, so a stray report never reaches status; a process manager over plain messages makes the check itself, with a correlation identifier and its own note of the step in flight.
limits.item3: When the steps are known before the message sets out and never depend on results, a process manager is more machinery than the job needs: a routing slip or a fixed pipeline does the same without central state. Reach for the manager when results choose the route, as the failed verification does at frame 5.
limits.item4: The analogy breaks in two places. DotLn's router keeps no record of its own: it reads status afresh each time, so the state lives in the log and the decision in the router, where the pattern keeps both in one component. And one drive runs one order, one phase at a time, while a process manager usually runs many instances at once and may send work down parallel legs.

item0.why: A routing slip is the choice when the sequence of steps is fixed before the message sets out: the list travels with the message and no central record is needed.

item1.why: For the trade-off between the two directly: what each can express, and where each is cheaper to run and to change.

item2.why: A correlation identifier is what a manager running many orders at once needs to tell whose report has just arrived.

item3.why: For what the central record costs: the bottleneck, the single point of control, and recovering its state after a crash.

item4.why: An aggregator joins parallel legs: when a process sends work to several steps at once, it collects their answers before the manager decides.

example.operator: merge, scan(fold), takeWhile(not stopped), map(phrase), delay(1)

notes.0: The operator has order {{order}} to drive. The router has no order, and the executor, the verifier and the reviewer are idle.
notes.1: The operator sends d, the drive that hands {{order}} to the router to take through every phase. The router starts a record of the order: nothing done, no failures.
notes.2: The router sends N, resume: next, to the executor, which starts building the order.
notes.3: The executor sends i, implementation-ready, back to the router. The router notes that the order is built and that verification comes next.
notes.4: The router sends V, resume: verify, to the verifier.
notes.5: The verifier sends x, a failed verification, to the router. The router counts {{failures}} failure of {{failureLimit}}; with fewer than {{failureLimit}}, a failure means repair.
notes.6: The router sends F, resume: fix, to the executor. A pass would have sent the order to the reviewer instead: the reply chose the step.
notes.7: The executor sends c, repair-complete, to the router, which calls for verification again.
notes.8: The router sends V, resume: verify, to the verifier a second time: the repair loop has gone round once.
notes.9: The verifier sends p, a passed verification, to the router, which calls for the final review.
notes.10: The router sends R, resume: final review, to the reviewer.
notes.11: The reviewer sends a, a passed final review, to the router. The order is ready to merge, which only the operator may do.
notes.12: The router sends M, its stop, to the operator, asking for the merge, and reads no more reports for this order.

example.caption: Time runs in frames, one message to a frame. drive$ is the operator starting the route; outcomes$ is what the executor, the verifier and the reviewer report to the router, in small letters; phrases$ is what the router sends, in capitals, each one frame after the message that called for it.

flow.caption: The boxes: the Operator starts the route and is the only one who may merge; the Router is the process manager, which keeps its record of the order and decides each next step; the Executor builds and repairs the order, the Verifier checks it and the Reviewer gives it a final review. The workers never send to each other: every line runs to or from the Router. Each token is one message, and d is the operator's drive. Capitals are the router's phrases, each telling one worker to start: N resume: next (build), V resume: verify, F resume: fix (repair), R resume: final review, and M the stop that asks the operator to merge. Small letters are the workers' reports back: i implementation-ready, x a failed verification, c repair-complete, p a passed verification and a a passed final review. The words in a box say what that box is doing; in the Router they are its record: the step it calls for or awaits, and how many verifications have failed of the {{failureLimit}} allowed. A token is green while it moves, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green.

intuition.text: The channel does the copying, not the sender. The planner publishes each order once and never learns who is listening; the topic keeps a list of its subscribers and gives each one a copy of its own, so nothing one session does with its copy can reach another's. The list that counts is the one at the moment of publishing, and the topic keeps no copy afterwards: a session that subscribes later hears only what is published after it joins.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public architecture document. DotLn is the operator's agentic platform, where agent sessions take roles such as planning and execution on work orders, and the document describes feedback agents that listen to the platform's stream of events, each deciding from its own trigger when to act, off the main thread, sometimes dispatching actions in turn. Picture the planner, the role that files work orders, publishing each new order on an Order topic, and three agent sessions subscribed to it, each deciding by its own trigger what the order means for it. A board, or an audit listener on the log, could subscribe beside them: the planner would publish exactly as before and the three sessions would hear no less. The Competing Consumers study sends the same orders to the same sessions over a queue, so the two differ only in how the channel delivers.

example.name: Four orders on a topic with three sessions
example.description: The planner publishes orders {orders} on the Order topic at frames 1, 3, 5 and 7, and keeps publishing whether or not anyone listens. The topic has {subscribers} subscribers, Sessions 1, 2 and 3, all subscribed from frame 0 to the end, and hands out each order's copies one frame after it is published. The Competing Consumers study sends the same orders at the same frames to the same three sessions over a queue.

step0.title: Add a subscriber to the list
step0.text: When a session subscribes, the topic adds it to its list. From then on it is given a copy of every order published; it is given nothing published before, because nothing was kept.

step1.title: Copy each publication to everyone on the list
step1.text: When the planner publishes an order, the topic puts one copy on the line of each session on the list at that moment, and makes no copy for anyone else. The planner publishes once whatever the list holds, so adding a subscriber changes nothing for the planner.

step2.title: Each copy belongs to its subscriber
step2.text: A session reads the copy on its own line once, and reading it takes nothing from the other sessions' lines. A session that reads slowly falls behind on its own line only.

step3.title: Keep nothing
step3.text: Once the copies are handed out, the topic forgets the order: after each step that hands out copies it is empty again. A session that was not on the list when the order was published never hears of it.

pseudocode.ordinary:
when a session subscribes:
  add it to the list of subscribers
  (it is given only what is published from now on)

when the planner publishes an order:
  for each session on the list right now:
    put a copy of the order on that session's own line

when a session reads the copy on its line:
  take that copy off its line
  (no other session's copy is touched)

after the copies are handed out:
  forget the order
  (a session that subscribes later never hears of it)

visual.textEquivalent: Step {step} on the Order topic: {moves}. Where the orders are: {held}. What each box does: {states}.

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is the Apache Software Foundation's open-source integration framework, and its documentation describes how Camel expresses many of the book's patterns, this one among them. Its page for this pattern is read here at the 4.22.x long-term-support release.
item0.explanation: Camel has no topic of its own for this: the page says the pattern comes from messaging components such as JMS, ActiveMQ, AMQP, Spring RabbitMQ and Camel's internal SEDA queues, and from cloud providers' messaging. Its example has one route send to a JMS topic and two further routes each consume from that same topic and pass what they receive to a different bean, so each bean is given every message the first route sends.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring project's implementation of the book's messaging model inside a Spring application, with channels and endpoints as objects in the application context. Its PublishSubscribeChannel is an in-process topic.
item1.explanation: The channel hands every message it is sent to each handler subscribed to it, calling the handlers one after another; it cannot be polled, so a subscriber must itself be a handler. The page places it with event messages meant as notification, as against document messages that one handler processes. Since version 3.0 a send counts as successful when at least minSubscribers subscribers are present, and that minimum defaults to 0, so publishing to nobody is not an error unless it is raised.

item2.relevance: RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker. Its getting-started tutorials build small Node.js programs against it, and the third builds publish/subscribe as a logging system in which every running receiver gets every log message.
item2.explanation: A fanout exchange copies every message it receives to every queue bound to it. Each receiver declares its own exclusive queue with a name the server chooses and binds it to the exchange, so each subscriber has a line of its own, deleted when its connection closes. The tutorial notes that a message is lost when no queue is yet bound to the exchange, and accepts that because its receivers want only the messages flowing while they run.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Publish-Subscribe Channel
item0.supports: The pattern's page in the public catalog: the channel takes messages in at one end and gives each subscriber an output channel of its own, each subscriber consumes its copy once, and a monitor listening on such a channel can log all its traffic while the flow it watches carries on unchanged. Its example notes that Google Cloud Pub/Sub gives each subscription on a topic its own copy, while subscribers sharing one subscription compete.

item1.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe and Woolf, Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 4: Messaging Channels, Publish-Subscribe Channel
item1.supports: The book covers the Publish-Subscribe Channel in chapter 4, Messaging Channels; the publisher's page lists that chapter in its contents.

item2.title: DotLn · Architecture, the agentic communication core (commit 9139d91)
item2.supports: The platform's architecture presents its agentic communication core as redux and RxJS applied to agents. In it, feedback agents listen to the stream of events and each decides from its own trigger when to act, working off the main thread and sometimes dispatching actions in turn. Files shared in the repository may carry messages at first, but canonical state lives in the append-only log.

item3.title: share.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item3.supports: At the installed version share's default connector is a plain Subject, every subscriber is subscribed to that Subject, and the source is subscribed only when a subscriber arrives and no connection exists, so all the sessions listen through one subscription to the planner's stream.

item4.title: Subject.ts in RxJS 7.8.2
item4.supports: A Subject's next hands the value to each of its current observers one after another in a single loop, so its subscribers receive a value in turn within the same call rather than from lines of their own.

item5.title: RxJS guide · Testing RxJS code with marble diagrams (source at 7.8.2)
item5.supports: The marble syntax this example and its spec share: a dash is one frame and a letter an emission, a hot observable behaves as though it is already running when the test begins, and subscription marbles given to expectObservable defer a subscriber to the frame of their caret, which is how a late subscriber is tested.

limits.item0: A subscriber that is not listening misses what is published, and nothing tells it so. Had Session 3 subscribed at frame {lateJoin}, after the copies of order 33 went out, it would have received only order 34: the topic kept no copy of the first three for it. When a subscriber must catch up after joining late or being away, use a Durable Subscriber, for which the channel keeps publications while it is gone, or record every publication in a Message Store it can read back.
limits.item1: A copy for every subscriber is the wrong delivery for work that must be done once. If each session takes a new order as a job to start, all three start order 31, and every order is worked three times. Use a Point-to-Point Channel with Competing Consumers, which the companion study runs on these same orders and sessions, so each order goes to one session.
limits.item2: Publishing succeeds whether or not anyone hears it. A topic with no subscribers, or with subscribers whose triggers all ignore an order, accepts the order and nothing happens: Spring Integration's channel reports a send to nobody as a success unless a minimum number of subscribers is set, and RabbitMQ's fanout exchange drops a message no queue is bound to. A sender that must know its order was taken up needs a reply or a queue, not a topic.
limits.item3: Copies multiply with listeners. Each publication becomes one copy per subscriber, so every subscriber added adds traffic for every later order. A broker gives each subscriber a line of its own, so a slow one falls behind alone; the RxJS reading has no such lines, because share's Subject hands each value to its subscribers one after another in the same call, and a subscriber that blocks holds up the ones after it.
limits.item4: The analogy breaks at the log. DotLn's architecture keeps its canonical state in an append-only log, so a session that starts late could read the events it missed: the platform's stream is closer to a channel backed by a Message Store than to the bare topic drawn here, where order 31 is gone for good once its copies are handed out.

item0.why: Competing Consumers is the choice when the three sessions should share the orders out, each order to one of them, rather than each hear every one; the companion study runs these same orders over a queue.

item1.why: A Point-to-Point Channel is the choice when each message is meant for exactly one receiver, whichever it turns out to be.

item2.why: A Durable Subscriber is the choice when a subscriber that is away or joins late must still be given what was published meanwhile.

item3.why: A Message Store is the choice when a reader needs the history of what was published, not only what arrives from now on.

item4.why: A Wire Tap is the choice for watching one point-to-point channel's traffic without turning that channel into a topic.

item5.why: A Recipient List is the choice when the sender, not the receivers, must decide who gets each message, naming the recipients itself.

notes.0: Sessions 1, 2 and 3 have subscribed to the Order topic. The planner has published nothing yet.
notes.1: The planner publishes order 31 to the Order topic, once. It does not know who is subscribed.
notes.2: The Order topic gives a copy of order 31 to Session 1, Session 2 and Session 3, and keeps no copy itself.
notes.3: The planner publishes order 32 to the Order topic.
notes.4: The Order topic gives a copy of order 32 to each of the {{subscribers}} sessions. Each session now has its own copies of orders 31 and 32.
notes.5: The planner publishes order 33 to the Order topic.
notes.6: The Order topic gives a copy of order 33 to each of the {{subscribers}} sessions.
notes.7: The planner publishes order 34 to the Order topic, exactly as it published order 31.
notes.8: The Order topic gives a copy of order 34 to each of the {{subscribers}} sessions. Every session has received every order: {{orders}} orders, {{copies}} copies.

example.caption: Time runs in frames. orders$ is what the planner publishes: a, b, c and d are orders 31, 32, 33 and 34. Each lane below the band is one session, subscribed from frame 0, and every session receives every order one frame after the planner publishes it.

flow.caption: Each token is one order: a is order 31, b 32, c 33 and d 34. The Planner is the role that files orders; the Order topic, drawn as a pipe, is the publish-subscribe channel; Sessions 1, 2 and 3 are {{subscribers}} agent sessions subscribed to it. A token inside the topic is an order it is about to copy, and the tokens inside a session are the copies that session has received. The words in a box say what that box does. A token is green while it moves, and a box a token leaves or reaches is outlined in green. The Planner publishes an order on one step, and on the next the topic hands out its copies, one to every session.

intuition.text: A recipient list works in two halves. First it decides, for this one message, who should have it; then it walks that list and hands each recipient its own copy. The list can change from one message to the next and can be empty, and it is worth keeping beside the message, because afterwards it is the only account of who was meant to receive what.
intuition.situation: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. Once an order's release has been tagged and published, release close brings every declared export sibling, a separate repository kept in step with each release, up to date: it fast-forwards the sibling's main branch to one checked commit, tags that commit with the release's tag name, gives the sibling its own Release, and notes each refresh in its close record. A close that publishes nothing new, such as one for a target order whose change landed in another repository, or one for an older version, updates no sibling. So the list is worked out per release from two sources, the declared siblings, which are configuration, and the close itself, which is the message, and it is kept with the dispatch.

example.name: Three release closes and the declared siblings
example.description: As an analogy, read against DotLn's public execution guide. Siblings {declaredFirst} are declared at step 1, and three closes, {closes}, arrive at steps 2, 4 and 7. WO-240 publishes v0.95.0. WO-241 is a target order, whose change landed in another repository, and publishes no release. At step 6 a third sibling is declared, so the declared siblings become {declaredLater}, and WO-242 then publishes v0.96.0. The recipient list works out each close's list when the close arrives and, the step after, writes the order and the list to the close record and sends each sibling on the list its own copy of the close on that sibling's main branch; the closes end at step 8.

step0.title: Keep the declared siblings
step0.text: Each declaration replaces the siblings the recipient list knows. It is read when a close passes, so a change applies to later closes only.

step1.title: Compute the list for this close
step1.text: A close that publishes a release goes to every sibling declared at that moment; a close that publishes none, as WO-241 does, gets an empty list.

step2.title: Record the list with the dispatch
step2.text: Write the order and its recipients to the close record, an empty list included, so the record shows who was meant to have each release.

step3.title: Send each recipient its own copy
step3.text: Walk the list and send each sibling a fresh, unchanged copy of the close on that sibling's own channel. A sibling not on the list hears nothing.

step4.title: End with the closes
step4.text: When the closes end, every sibling's channel and the close record end with them.

pseudocode.ordinary:
on each declaration:
  declared = the siblings it names

on each close:
  if the close publishes a release:
    recipients = declared, as it stands now
  otherwise:
    recipients = nobody

  write (the close's order, recipients) to the close record

  for each sibling in recipients:
    send a fresh copy of the close on that sibling's main

when the closes end:
  end every sibling's channel and the close record

visual.textEquivalent: Step {step}: {moves}. Each sibling's main is its own channel, and every close's list goes to the close record. Now {states}; {held}.

item0.relevance: Apache Camel is an open-source Java integration framework whose routes are assembled from the integration patterns by name. Its Recipient List EIP, built on its Multicast EIP, is documented here for the 4.22 long-term-support line.
item0.explanation: An expression computes the endpoints for each message: a constant for a fixed list, or a header the message carries for a dynamic one, as a comma-separated string or a collection. Camel sends to them one after another by default, or in parallel, and can aggregate the replies into a single message. When one recipient fails it carries on to the rest by default; with stopOnException it stops there, so the recipients after the failure get nothing. onPrepare can deep-clone each copy before it is sent, and ignoreInvalidEndpoints skips an endpoint that cannot be created.

item1.relevance: Spring Integration is the Spring portfolio's implementation of the integration patterns for Java applications. Its router implementations page describes the RecipientListRouter it ships.
item1.explanation: The router sends each message to a list of channels configured up front, and a selector expression per recipient, such as a test on the payload or on a header, decides whether that channel is on the list for a given message. Since version 4.1 recipients can be added and removed at run time through a control bus or JMX, so a router may start with none; a message no recipient takes goes to the default output channel if one is set, and otherwise raises a MessageDeliveryException. It also offers apply-sequence and ignore-send-failures settings.

item2.relevance: Apache Synapse is the Apache Software Foundation's mediation engine and enterprise service bus. RecipientListEndpoint.java, read at the Apache-Synapse-3.0.2 tag, is its recipient list.
item2.explanation: send takes its recipients from configured child endpoints, from cluster members, or from an expression evaluated on each message into a comma-separated list of addresses, keeping the endpoints it creates for those addresses in a small least-recently-used pool. For each recipient that is ready to send it clones the message context and stamps the clone with its position and the list's size, for an aggregator to use later. A recipient that is not ready is skipped, an expression that yields no address sends nothing, and a failing recipient is logged and reported as a failure.

item0.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns · Recipient List
item0.supports: For each message the pattern works out who should receive it and then delivers it on every one of those recipients' channels; the page describes this as two steps that implementations often merge, building the list and then walking it to send each recipient a copy, and says the content is normally left as it was.

item1.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe and Woolf, Addison-Wesley, 2003) · Chapter 7: Message Routing, Recipient List
item1.supports: The book covers the Recipient List in Chapter 7, Message Routing.

item2.title: DotLn execution guide · Workflow closeout and releases
item2.supports: Once a release's tag and Release exist, DotLn's release close brings every declared export sibling up to date: it fast-forwards the sibling's main branch to one commit it has checked, exporting the kit to it the first time, tags that commit with core's release tag name and gives the sibling a Release of its own. A close that publishes nothing new, whether for a target order or an older version, updates no sibling. The close record, release-close.json, and its summary note every refresh; a close is not finished while a refresh is blocked, a refused refresh is retried by running the same command again, and a retry that meets a sibling's existing tag and Release reports that sibling current.

limits.item0: There is no transaction across the recipients. Copies go out one by one, so when one recipient refuses, those before it already have the message and those after it may or may not, depending on whether the sender carries on or stops. A safe retry sends to the whole list again, so every recipient has to treat a copy it already holds as done. The guide's close does exactly this: a refused refresh blocks the close, and the retry reports an already refreshed sibling as current, an Idempotent Receiver at each sibling.
limits.item1: The list is computed when the message passes. Sibling C is declared at step 6 and receives nothing of v0.95.0, which went out at step 3; it hears only from WO-242 on. A recipient that must catch up needs the current state or a stored history, not the recipient list; the guide's refresh, for its part, can export the kit, the platform's shared files, to a sibling for the first time, which hands a new sibling the current state rather than the releases it missed.
limits.item2: An empty list has to be visible. WO-241 reaches nobody, which is right for a target order but looks the same, from any sibling, as a list computed wrongly. Recording every list with its dispatch, the empty ones included, is what lets someone check it afterwards.
limits.item3: In memory a copy is only as deep as you make it. The RxJS reading spreads each close into a new object for each sibling, so one sibling changing its copy cannot change another's, but anything nested inside would still be shared. A framework that sends real copies, such as Camel with onPrepare, settles this for you.
limits.item4: The sender has to know every recipient. When receivers should decide for themselves, a Publish-Subscribe Channel with a filter on each receiver needs no central list, at the cost of no single record of who was meant to receive what. When the copies are requests whose answers must be combined, the list is only the first half of a Scatter-Gather and needs an Aggregator after it.
limits.item5: The analogy breaks where the platform waits. DotLn's refresh is no fire-and-forget copy: each sibling gets its own commit and Release, checked before the push, and a close is done only when no refresh blocker remains. In the pattern the recipient list's work ends once each copy is on its channel; waiting until every recipient has finished, as the close does, is a further step the pattern leaves to whatever follows it.

item0.why: Reach for a Content-Based Router when each message has exactly one right destination, so no list is needed.

item1.why: Reach for a Publish-Subscribe Channel when every subscriber should get every message and the receivers, not the sender, decide who listens.

item2.why: Reach for Scatter-Gather when the recipients answer and their answers must be combined into one result.

item3.why: Reach for an Aggregator after the recipient list when its copies come back as replies that belong together.

item4.why: Reach for an Idempotent Receiver at each recipient whenever a failed dispatch is retried by sending to the whole list again.

item5.why: Read the robust-delivery trade-off for the two ways to make every recipient get its copy: send all the copies in one transaction, or let receivers ignore duplicates.

item6.why: Reach for a Dynamic Router when recipients should register and withdraw their own interest at run time instead of being written into one list.

example.operator: withLatestFrom(declared$), map to a list, delay(1), share
